how_checked: Nine research lenses read the web on 2026-09-22 and returned 240 claims; each lens was tidied to at most 22, duplicates were folded across lenses (39), and every load-bearing or licence claim was checked twice by independent agents told to refute it: fact and drift for facts and capabilities, text and drift for licences. A non-licence claim that any check refuted in part carries the checker's narrower wording and the status corrected; a licence claim whose two checks disagreed is unsettled. Minor claims stayed unchecked.

claims.claim: Card hair is built in layers from the scalp outward, thick to thin (slosh), with at least three layers: an opaque base layer that covers the scalp completely (Giovannini, Sorici, Porfyridou, Hansen), one or more breakup layers of progressively less opaque cards (Giovannini "at least 1 or 2 more times", Sorici, Porfyridou, Hansen), then transitional hairline cards and flyaways (Giovannini, Sorici, Porfyridou; slosh lists cap, mostly opaque base strands, filler strands, thin strand cards, flyaways). Giovannini groups cards into clumps of 2 to 3 throughout all layers; Hansen uses tent-shaped clusters of 3 to 5 cards, mostly 3, with the base card most opaque. Hansen starts from the innermost layer with big, blocky, fully opaque planes. Giovannini bakes ambient occlusion into the card vertices layer by layer once all layers are built; Scheuermann (GDC 2004) uses several layers of patches with per-vertex ambient occlusion. No source states a hairline-to-crown placement order.
claims.as_first_reported: Card hair is layered scalp outward, thick to thin, at least three layers: an opaque base covering the scalp, one or more progressively more transparent breakup layers of 2 to 3 card clumps, then hairline transition cards and flyaways, placed biggest clumps first from hairline to crown, with ambient occlusion baked into card vertices per layer (slosh, Giovannini, Porfyridou, Scheuermann).

checks.evidence: SUPPORTED parts. slosh (Polycount comment 2655349, 2018-10-09): "going thick to thin as you go outward is a good call. You want some sort of cap under ur cards...this can be separate piece of geo or painted straight onto the head. For me, I like to have several layers...the cap, base strands that are mostly opaque, filler strands that have more alpha but aren't just a few strands, thin strand cards which will just have less strands and can be intersected(these make up the bulk), and flyaways to break up the surface and silhouette." Giovannini (80.lv tips): "First, the individual cards are combined and setup as hair clumps consisting of 2-3 cards each." / "Start out by creating an opaque base layer blocking in the overall structure and flow of the hair carefully following the references, while being sure to get good coverage over the scalp of the character's head. Then begin laying down a breakup layer using less opaque cards following the general flow and structure of the base layer" / "This step is repeated at least 1 or 2 more times using less opaque hair cards each time for each layer." / "The final layers are also used to work out the transition areas along the hairline and introduce stray hairs and flyaways." / "Once all layers are constructed, the ambient occlusion is baked into the vertices of the hair cards on a layer-by-layer basis". Sorici (Marmoset): "The first layer is just a bunch of hair cards that establish the hairline, mass, and direction. This layer should be thick so that it covers the scalp completely, with no visible gaps." / "The second layer has thinner hair strands that add volume, intricacy, and breakup the monotony of the hair." / "The third layer is composed of transitional and flyaway hairs." Porfyridou (80.lv real-time): "the base layer is used mainly to cover the scalp and has the opaquest texture assigned on while next layers are more transparent" / "one strand for the flyaways and a couple for the short transitional hair". Hansen (80.lv CGMA): "I started the work from the bottom or innermost layers and made sure I basically have the hairstyle in place with the big, blocky and completely opaque hair planes." / "the bottom layer of hair is 100 opaque." / "Most of them are just 3 cards where the one at the base of it is the most opaque, and the 2 on top are slightly more transparent." (clusters of "3-5 hair cards"). Scheuermann (GDC 2004 slide 5): "Several layers of patches to approximate volumetric qualities of hair" / "Ambient occlusion to approximate self-shadowing - Per vertex". NOT FOUND in any source: "placed biggest clumps first from hairline to crown". The word "crown" appears in none of the five sources; "biggest" in Giovannini only as "The biggest tip I can offer". Nearest support is Hansen's big opaque planes first, innermost layer outward, and Sorici's first layer establishing the hairline; neither gives a hairline-to-crown placement order.
checks.notes: Refuted in part, not wholesale: the layer structure (opaque scalp-covering base, progressively more transparent breakup layers, transitional hairline cards and flyaways, at least three layers, thick to thin outward) is well supported across all five sources. Four defects. (1) "placed biggest clumps first from hairline to crown" is in none of the sources; "hairline to crown" is invented. (2) "2 to 3 card clumps" is Giovannini alone and he applies it to all cards, not to breakup layers specifically; Hansen's clusters are 3 to 5 (mostly 3), so the range is narrower than the sources. (3) "ambient occlusion baked into card vertices per layer" is Giovannini alone; Scheuermann says per-vertex AO on layered patches, not per-layer baking, and no Scheuermann URL was in the researcher's source list (I located the GDC 2004 slides at an Oregon State mirror; the AMD developer URLs are dead). (4) Attribution mismatch: the parenthetical names slosh, Giovannini, Porfyridou, Scheuermann, but two of the five given sources are by Sorici and Hansen, who are unnamed, while Porfyridou supports only the base-opaque/next-layers-transparent and flyaway/transitional points, not clump sizes or AO. Also minor: slosh says base strands are "mostly opaque" with a separate cap (geometry or painted on the head) under them, so "opaque base covering the scalp" is Giovannini/Sorici/Hansen wording, not slosh's. Web search budget for this session was exhausted (200/200) before this check, so no searches were run; all verification is from fetched pages. Polycount blocks direct fetches with a CAPTCHA; the forum API and Wayback copy agree word for word. Giovannini groups cards into clumps of 2 to 3 throughout all layers; Hansen uses tent-shaped clusters of 3 to 5 cards, mostly 3, with the base card most opaque. Hansen starts from the innermost layer with big, blocky, fully opaque planes. Giovannini bakes ambient occlusion into the card vertices layer by layer once all layers are built; Scheuermann (GDC 2004) uses several layers of patches with per-vertex ambient occlusion. Sorici, marmoset.co: "The first layer ... should be thick so that it covers the scalp completely, with no visible gaps." / "The second layer has thinner hair strands" / "The third layer is composed of transitional and flyaway hairs." Hansen, 80.lv (004adk): "I started the work from the bottom or innermost layers ... with the big, blocky and completely opaque hair planes" / "for the first layer ... fewer but big clumps, and then, in the second and third use, higher and higher values to get smaller subclumps" / "taking 3-5 hair cards ... Most of them are just 3 cards where the one at the base of it is the most opaque" / "the bottom layer of hair is 100 opaque". Scheuermann, GDC 2004 slide 5: "Several layers of patches to approximate volumetric qualities of hair. Ambient occlusion to approximate self-shadowing - Per vertex"; SIGGRAPH 2004 sketch: "As a simple approximation for hair self-shadowing, we store an ambient occlusion term per vertex. This term is computed in a pre-processing step." UNSUPPORTED PARTS. (1) "from hairline to crown": the word "crown" appears in none of the eleven documents read; Giovannini places hairline cards LAST ("The final layers are also used to work out the transition areas along the hairline"), Sorici's FIRST layer "establish[es] the hairline, mass, and direction"; neither states a hairline-to-crown sweep. (2) "biggest clumps first": only Hansen says this (big blocky planes first, "fewer but big clumps" then "smaller subclumps"); none of the four names in the claim's attribution says it. (3) "2 to 3 card clumps": Giovannini only, and he applies it to all layers including the base, not specifically to breakup layers; Hansen gives 3 to 5, mostly 3. (4) "AO baked into card vertices per layer": "layer-by-layer" is Giovannini alone; Scheuermann has per-vertex AO with no per-layer step; Sorici and Parker bake AO to a texture map instead ("use aiUtility to bake the AO map"; "bake a Normal and an Ambient Occlusion map"). (5) Scheuermann attribution: his two documents support only "several layers" and "per-vertex AO"; nothing on thick-to-thin, an opaque scalp-covering base, clumps, hairline transition cards or flyaways. His "inside to outside draw order" is a render-time sort, not an authoring order. (6) slosh's base strands are "mostly opaque" with a separate "cap" (geometry or painted scalp) beneath them; the claim collapses cap and base into one "opaque base covering the scalp".
checks.notes: Verdict is refuted in part: the layering scheme itself has five independent artist sources plus Scheuermann, but the exact wording bundles in a placement order ("from hairline to crown") found in no source, a per-layer AO step and a 2 to 3 card clump size that each rest on Giovannini alone, and an attribution to Scheuermann that covers only two of the sentence's seven assertions. Drift and conflation found while checking: (a) the WebFetch summariser swapped the bylines of the two 80.lv URLs (it called 004adk Porfyridou and creating-hair-for-real-time-projects Hansen); raw HTML shows the reverse, and the researcher's Porfyridou quote is real and sits at creating-hair-for-real-time-projects. (b) The summariser reported the Marmoset article as 2025-12-19; the page's JSON-LD datePublished is 2018-11-06, so the later date is presumably a modification date. (c) The 80.lv article dates (2018-04-05, 2018-06-19, 2019-02-22) come from the summariser and were not re-verified from raw HTML; the two that were attributed to swapped authors may themselves be swapped. (d) The Scheuermann PDFs are gone from developer.amd.com (301 to a documentation hub); they were read from Wayback captures of 2017-01-01 and 2017-08-11. (e) polycount.com serves 403 to non-browser clients but its Vanilla JSON API is open. Limits: the session's WebSearch budget was exhausted before this check began, and DuckDuckGo (202 challenge) and Bing (no result links in the returned HTML) could not be scraped by curl, so the hunt for a second source was confined to tutorials linked from the polycount wiki: Tosca (block in the main shape, duplicate one clump) and Parker (layer the strips, bake an AO map) neither confirm nor contradict the scheme. Sorici's three-layer account is the only one matching "at least three layers" exactly; slosh lists five, Hansen four, Giovannini three or more. Corrected wording: Card hair is built in several layers from the scalp outward, thick to thin: an opaque or near-opaque base layer that covers the scalp (slosh adds a separate cap under it, as geometry or a painted scalp), one or more progressively more transparent breakup layers, then hairline transition cards and flyaways as the final layer (slosh 2018, Giovannini 2018, Porfyridou 2018, Sorici 2018, Hansen; at least three layers in every account). Giovannini builds every layer from clumps of 2 to 3 cards and bakes ambient occlusion into the card vertices layer by layer; Hansen uses clusters of 3 to 5, mostly 3, and places the biggest clumps first. Scheuermann (ATI, GDC and SIGGRAPH 2004) independently describes hair as several layers of polygon patches with a precomputed per-vertex ambient occlusion term, but says nothing about opacity ordering, clumps or flyaways. No source read places cards "from hairline to crown".

claims.claim: Hansen (80.lv, 2019) builds placement clusters of 3 to 5 cards in a tent-like shape, most often 3, with the card at the base the most opaque and the 2 on top slightly more transparent, and places near single hairs as a flyaway layer. Cecot (gamesartist.co.uk, 2021) uses 3 cards per hair card set in most cases and 2 cards for flyaway sets; he does not describe the set's profile or a per-card opacity order, and says he tries to prevent cards crossing each other when placing them. Epic's Hair Card Generator defines a multi-card clump as a group of three hair cards (an optional advanced setting) and a flyaway as one card with a single strand projected on it. arXiv 2505.18805 offers an optional "crossed cards" extension that generates a pair of cards per cluster at a 90-degree angle. No source was supplied for Jerabek, so that attribution is unverified.
claims.as_first_reported: A hair clump is two to five cards, most often three, in a tent or crossed profile with the innermost card the most opaque and the two on top more transparent (Hansen, Jerabek, Cecot); Epic's Hair Card Generator likewise builds three cards per clump, flyaways are one- or two-card single strands, and arXiv 2505.18805 pairs cards at 90 degrees.

checks.evidence: Hansen (80.lv, interview dated 22 February 2019): "This is done by taking 3-5 hair cards and placing them together in a tent-like shape to add more volume to the hair no matter the angle you look at it from. Most of them are just 3 cards where the one at the base of it is the most opaque, and the 2 on top are slightly more transparent." and "...until you get to place pretty much single hairs for a flyaway layer." Cecot (gamesartist.co.uk, 07 February 2021): "In most cases, I used 3 cards to get 1 full hair card set. For the flyaway hair, I used 2 cards instead, as it's not so important to get more volume in their case, but rather to get rounded shapes later." and, on placement, "When placing hair cards, I do my best to prevent hair from crossing each other." Epic UE docs: Glossary "Multi-Card Clumps: Multiple cards (3) per strand clump to give the appearance of volume."; filter settings "A multi-card clump is a group of three hair cards that represent a volume of hair." and "A flyaway is a card with a single strand projected on it, used for details."; advanced option "Multi-Card Clumps: Generates three cards per strand clump to give the appearance of volume." arXiv 2505.18805 (Zheng et al., "Auto Hair Card Extraction for Smooth Hair with Differentiable Rendering"), section 4.6 Extensions, introduced as one of "two additional optional features": "for each cluster, we generate a pair of hair cards placed at a 90-degree angle to each other, creating the illusion of volumetric hair using flat geometry" and "we simply create an additional card perpendicular to the primary card at each segment by rotating both n_k,j and t_k,j over 90 degrees, giving a crossed configuration." The name "Jerabek" appears in none of the four sources supplied.
checks.notes: Refuted in part, not in whole. Each number in the claim traces to a source, but the composite sentence over-attributes: (1) "two to five" merges Hansen's 3-5 with Cecot's 2-card flyaway sets, so 2 is a flyaway count, not a clump count in any source; (2) "tent" is Hansen only and "crossed" is the arXiv paper only, yet both are attributed to the three artists, and Cecot explicitly avoids crossing cards during placement; (3) the "innermost most opaque, two on top more transparent" ordering is Hansen only (his wording is "at the base of it"), Cecot gives no per-card opacity order; (4) Jerabek is not in any supplied source and could not be searched (WebSearch budget exhausted, DuckDuckGo returned a bot challenge), so "not found"; (5) "flyaways are one- or two-card single strands" fuses UE's one-card single-strand definition with Cecot's 2-card flyaway sets, and Cecot does not say his 2-card flyaways are single strands (his flyaway textures are "few hairs or even just a single one"); (6) the arXiv 90-degree pairing is an optional extension, not the paper's default output. The UE three-card clump statement and the arXiv 90-degree statement are confirmed verbatim. All quotes above were taken from the raw HTML fetched with curl on 2026-09-22, not from a summary. checks.notes: Refuted in part, on attribution and qualifiers only; the substance holds and appears in more than one write-up. (1) Conflation: the parenthetical "(Hansen, Jerabek, Cecot)" is attached to "tent or crossed profile with the innermost card the most opaque and the two on top more transparent", but Cecot states none of that; he gives only "3 cards" per set and "2 cards" for flyaways. "Innermost ... two on top" is Hansen's wording alone; Jerabek gives "one opaque card ... crossed with two semi-sparse ones" without an inner/outer order. (2) Drift: "Epic's Hair Card Generator likewise builds three cards per clump" is true of the Multi-Card Clumps setting, which the docs list under "Advanced Options: Optional settings"; no default value is stated on the page, and arXiv 2505.18805 Fig. 5 labels the UE auto tool's output "single cards". (3) Drift: the arXiv 90-degree pairing is one of "two additional optional features" (Sec. 4.6), not the paper's base method, which fits one card per cluster. (4) "Flyaways are one- or two-card single strands" merges UE (one card, single strand) with Cecot (two cards; he does not say single strand) and Hansen (single hairs, no card count); acceptable as a synthesis if attributed that way. (5) "Two to five": Hansen alone gives 3-5; the lower bound of 2 comes from Giovannini (2-3), Jerabek's two-card sparse strands and Cecot's two-card flyaways. (6) Independence: Hansen's piece is a CGMA "Hair Creation for Games" student project and Giovannini's is from the same CGMA course; Jerabek explicitly took her layering from Cecot; so there are roughly three lineages (CGMA course, Cecot/Jerabek, Epic docs) plus the arXiv paper, not one blog post. (7) The researcher's Hansen quote is verbatim accurate. The researcher gave no source for Jerabek; the 80.lv Natalie Jerabek interview (19 September 2025) is the only Jerabek hair-card write-up found and it does support the crossed three-card clump. (8) Tooling: the session's WebSearch budget was already exhausted, so searches went through search.brave.com by curl; DuckDuckGo returned a bot challenge and Bing returned irrelevant results. Corrected wording: A hair clump is two to five cards, most often three. Hansen (80.lv) builds clusters of "3-5 hair cards ... in a tent-like shape", most "just 3 cards where the one at the base of it is the most opaque, and the 2 on top are slightly more transparent", with "single hairs for a flyaway layer". Jerabek (80.lv, 2025) builds "strands of three cards: one opaque card carefully crossed with two semi-sparse ones" in a "criss-cross profile", plus a breakup layer of "two sparse cards crossing each other"; she credits Cecot's breakdown for her layering. Cecot (gamesartist.co.uk) uses "3 cards to get 1 full hair card set" and "2 cards" for flyaway hair, and says nothing about clump profile or opacity order. Giovannini (80.lv, 2018) uses "hair clumps consisting of 2-3 cards each" with progressively less opaque layers. Epic's Hair Card Generator (UE 5.8 docs, Experimental) defines "a multi-card clump" as "a group of three hair cards" through its Multi-Card Clumps advanced option, and "a flyaway" as "a card with a single strand projected on it"; the docs do not state whether the option is on by default, and arXiv 2505.18805 describes the UE auto tool's output as "single cards". arXiv 2505.18805v2 offers crossed cards as an optional extension (Sec. 4.6): "for each cluster, we generate a pair of hair cards placed at a 90-degree angle to each other".

claims.claim: In the arXiv 2505.18805 differentiable-rendering pipeline, fidelity against a 40K-strand reference falls as cards are removed, PSNR 19.38 and LPIPS 0.138 at 200 cards, 18.51 and 0.165 at 100, 17.99 and 0.184 at 50, so halving cards from 200 to 100 costs about 0.9 dB in the paper's own renders.

Cards are placed with an S-curve and a curved root, never dead straight, while waviness lives in the geometry and the texture strokes stay straight and thin: Hansen 'always get a nice S-shape on your cards', Parker adds 'a slight curve to the top' of the strip primitive, Ortolani keeps textures 'generally straight'.

The 'spaghetti' or straw look is diagnosed on a Polycount critique thread as a texture 'way too dense and straight on far too few planes' (Neox) plus faceted vertex normals (thomasp), not as too few strands.

Cards go only where they add silhouette or volume and need not all grow from the scalp (Hansen: 'It doesnt have to grow directly out of the head from everywhere'), and density is judged by checking the base layer alone in the engine for see-throughs, gaps and texture repetition before adding layers (Zatorska).

Hairline and parting get their own short, sparse transitional cards in the final layers and the most attention: Dubey 'Hairline & Parting ... require your utmost attention', Jerabek 'placed dense haircards around the scalp and at the split of the bangs', Squara uses 'Short cards' for 'transition areas', and Epic's generator has a card group for hairline short hairs.

A hair cap sits under the cards: either a separate piece of geometry or hair painted straight onto the head (slosh, polycount 2018). Zatorska says "mostly short male hair" requires a hair cap mesh and texture, and that when using a cap mesh one should plan the transition between cap texture and cards using low-density cards; Turk uses the haircap "as a base layer to help with the transition between the scalp and cards" and finds it "very effective with a buzzed haircut". Fades are not mentioned by any source.

claims.claim: Long hair is built from the silhouette inward, wide backing strips first and thin breakup cards last, with texture strips of different lengths per region, and is placed by hand: Parker 'Start by laying down the underlying hair and working your way up', Cecot 'there is no better way than just manually placing every single hair card'.

The standard performance levers are minimising fully transparent texture area and dropping flyaways at distance: Sosa 'The fewer areas with full transparency, the better for the engine', Verhoolen 'The top layer with flyaway-hair can be switched off in the first LOD pretty quickly', and VSQUAD suggests LOD1 at '40-60% of cards'.

Curly hair is built from three to four card parts per curl with eight to ten curl variations, the first three layers recreating the volume and layers four and five adding 'chaotic curls' (Sosa), while Squara separates 'Big Curl Cards', sparse 'Layering Cards', transition cards, single-plane 'Facade Curl Cards' and flyaways.

Stylised (Overwatch or Arcane type) hair in the breakdowns found is solid sculpted locks with anisotropic shading rather than alpha cards, Vila building 'flakes' from curve tubes and Zavala dynameshing strands with creases to mimic card ends, and the one stylised card generator found (Murska, geometry nodes) uses V-profile cards laid in opaque-to-wisp passes.

Zatorska keeps card width constant within a layer and wider nearer the scalp, thinner low-density cards on top, so cards can swap atlas slots without changing rendered thickness; she sculpts a low-poly reference to plan flow, parting, volume and width, checks the first layer in engine before adding complexity, and no source gives width in centimetres.

checks.evidence: Zatorska 40NN (Article / 14 January 2022), section "3. Create the hair texture": "Create clumps with different hair amount – density. I tend to use cards with a more dense texture as the base layer and place them closer to the hair scalp. On the top layer, I use the cards with lower density and some distinctive hair variations (like waves or gaps between strands). ... Keep each strand the same width – or have few types of width. Make hair cards that are closer to the scalp wider, and others thinner – but the same width for each group (layer). This will help easily switch UV space for hair cards (to use texture variation where it is necessary) and keep the rendered hair thickness the same for all cards." Section "2. Sculpted hair for reference": "To answer these questions, I started with the sculpted mesh in ZBrush. ... The sculpted hair doesn't need to be detailed, I kept it simple and low poly, I've spent 20 mins on it max. The main goal is to design the hairstyle shape (the silhouette), establish the hair strands' flow, and estimate the width of the hair cards." The questions (section 1) include "How does the hair flow? In what direction? What is the shape of hair parting? ... Is it thick or thin?". Section "5. Place the hair cards": "I usually place the first layer of cards and check the mesh in the engine. It allows me to spot the mistakes/see-throughs/gaps/texture repetitions and fix them before the card structure becomes complex." Zatorska 9BDv (29 May 2020) repeats all of this with "(level)" for "(layer)", and its planning questions add "What is the volume – the amount of hair?". Neither Zatorska page contains any centimetre or unit figure for card width. arXiv 2505.18805 Section 4.2 "Card Geometry Fitting", Eq. 1: "we calculate the maximum distance from s̄_{k,j} to all corresponding strand samples within the cluster along the binormal direction such that: W_{k,j} = max_{S_i in G_k} |(s_{i,j} − s̄_{k,j}) · b_{k,j}|. Then, the card is constructed by connecting all p±_{k,j} = s̄_{k,j} ± W_{k,j} b_{k,j}"; the paper never uses the term "half-width", gives no units, and says "The user-defined per-strand hair width is denoted as w_i" with no value; "Zatorska" does not appear in it. The 3d.sk page contains no "width", "wider", "cm" or "centimetre" text.

"No source gives width in centimetres" holds for all four cited URLs. Two citation problems that do not change the verdict: (1) the blog.3d.sk URL is not a Helena Hansen article; the string "Helena" appears nowhere in its HTML. It is a republished 80.lv interview titled "Voluminous Hair: Tips and Tricks" with Jeff Hindsbøl Hansen (canonical https://80.lv/articles/004adk-005cg-cgma-student-project-voluminous-hair, not opened), about a CGMA course; it says only that the innermost layer is "big, blocky and completely opaque hair planes" with "more transparent and lusher hair cards on top", and it never mentions card width or Zatorska, so it contributes nothing to HAIR-013 and should be dropped or re-attributed. checks.notes: Drift and conflation checks. (1) Two ArtStation URLs are two versions of one article by one author, not two sources: 9BDv "Real-time Hair Workflows" (image assets timestamped 2020-05-29) and 40NN "Real-time Hair Creation Workflow" (14 January 2022). The claim's "(layer)" wording matches the 2022 version; the 2020 version says "(level)". The 9BDv page now opens with "UPDATE: Please check my newer version ... on my website Realtimehair.com", so the source has moved a third time; that newest copy could not be reached from here by any route, so whether its wording changed or added a unit is unverified. (2) The width rule sits in a bullet list headed "When creating the hair texture, I followed these principles", but the sentence itself says "Make hair cards that are closer to the scalp wider", so attributing it to card width is correct. (3) "thinner low-density cards on top" joins two separate sentences (density: dense base near scalp, lower density on the top layer; width: closer to scalp wider, "others thinner"); the join is faithful but the source never literally pairs "thinner" with "top layer". (4) "atlas slots" paraphrases "switch UV space"; "volume" comes from the 2020 version's planning question, while the 2022 version says "shape (the silhouette)". (5) Second independent source: Hansen (3d.sk, 16 Nov 2022, reposting her own Twitter thread) independently says the base layer uses "your thickest and most dense cards", "Be mindful of not making the cards too wide", and the breakup layer should "Keep using nice narrow cards ... using your less dense cards", which corroborates dense base / less dense narrower cards above, but she does not state constant width per layer or the UV-swap rationale. Those two points appear only in Zatorska's article, so they are single-author. The session's web search budget was exhausted (200 of 200) before this check, so no further search for an independent source was possible. (6) arXiv 2505.18805 (Zheng et al., "Auto Hair Card Extraction for Smooth Hair with Differentiable Rendering") never uses the phrase "half-width"; Eq. (1) is a half-extent by construction, and per-strand width w_i is "user-defined" with no value in the text. A tighter wording that avoids the joins: "Zatorska (2020 and 2022 versions of the same article) puts denser cards nearer the scalp and lower-density cards on the top layer, makes cards nearer the scalp wider and the rest thinner with one width per group (layer, called level in 2020), so UV space can be switched without changing rendered thickness; a quick low-poly ZBrush sculpt fixes silhouette, flow and card width, after planning questions that include parting (and, in 2020, volume); she checks the first card layer in the engine before the structure gets complex. None of the four cited pages gives a card width in centimetres; the newest copy on realtimehair.com was not reachable." Verbatim quotes above keep the source's own dashes.

claims.claim: Epic's UE5 Hair Card Generator (Experimental plugin) builds clumps of three cards and organises generation by card groups with per-group Num Clumps, Num Triangles, Num Flyaways, Num Textures, Strand Width and Max Vertical Segments, run as a White Core Layer (low clumps and triangles, wide cards for scalp coverage) then Mid, Top, Flyaway and Short Hairs layers; no defaults documented.

Placement is the skill-bound stage, StraySpark putting it at '4-12 hours' per character, and automation is regarded as inferior to hand placement below roughly 6k to 8k triangles: Zatorska 'When you work with low poly hair (under 6-8k) the best result give the manual placing of hair cards', and Ortolani finds generated cards 'never as clean'.

Published game-res card-hair budgets: Zatorska says developers of AAA and indie scale "usually keep the hair model in a range of 4k to 20k triangles" and that manual placement works best under 10k tris; for one RPG (The Colony Ship, Iron Tower Studio) her hair had to be "up to 4k tris", with manual placement suiting "2-4k tris". VSQUAD: a typical realistic card hairstyle is "200-400 planes" (elsewhere in the same article "150-400 hair cards"). StraySpark: a good real-time hairstyle "lands in the low hundreds of cards". Turk's buzzed, short and long set: "9,018 (Single Sided) 18,036 (Double Sided)" triangles for the hair cards. One polycount forum reply gives "17616 tris for that one character" for an unnamed whole Genshin Impact character (not hair alone). Epic's MetaHuman LOD specification lists "Hair Style Card Vertices" of 30,000 at LOD0 falling to 1,500 at LOD4 (mesh hair of 500 to 100 vertices at LOD5 to LOD7). The Reallusion 40,000-face hair cap is unsourced and was not found.

claims.claim: Flat-card vertex normals are replaced by normals transferred from the head mesh itself (short styles), a proxy mesh, or an enclosing sphere: Parker (3D Artist, 2015) does it with Maya's Transfer Attributes and says 3ds Max has scripts for it; leslievdb (Polycount thread 153172, May 2015) says "create a sphere around your hairmesh" and run the 3ds Max Normal Thief script (scriptspot). In Blender the equivalent is the Data Transfer modifier with Face Corner Data > Custom Normals; the one worked example found (Yarsa Labs, 2022, a stylised bush with a sphere as source, not hair) uses the default "Nearest Corner and Best Matching Face Normal" mapping, and the Blender 4.5 manual lists nearest-face and projected-face interpolated mappings as options without any hair guidance. Murska transfers normals from the base mesh to fur cards in Blender but names no modifier or mapping. The normal map is baked from straight hair so flow comes from card direction: jfitch in the same Polycount thread ("bake your normals with the hair straight ... (2) In the same thread the original poster (Croftyness, 2015-05-28T09:12:40Z) replied "I tried both of those methods but it didn't seem to work. I think it's a normal map baking problem." (4) "Normal Thief" is a family of three MAXScripts (2004 NormalThief.ms by Mauricio B. Gehling, the one leslievdb linked; 2010 SlideNormalThief, now unavailable per the polycount wiki; 2014 NoorsNormalThief). The scriptspot page is currently behind a Vercel security checkpoint (429) and was not opened. (5) The "Parker" source is a polycount-wiki backup PDF (printed 7/30/2015) of a 3dartistonline.com article whose byline is Steve Holmes writing up Tom Parker's tutorial; the original URL is dead and only archived. (7) The claim's kind "fact" mixes documented tool facts (Blender manual, Normal Thief's function) with practitioner tips from one 2015 magazine tutorial and one 2015 forum thread; a register entry should say "practitioner technique, two independent 2015 sources, one of them a forum thread whose OP reported it did not fix their case", not a documented fact. Blender's Data Transfer modifier transfers custom normals with Nearest Face Interpolated or Projected Face Interpolated face-corner mapping (4.5 manual), documented for foliage (Yarsa Labs 2022) and fur (Murska 2026), not specifically for hair cards." claims.claim: Hero and offline-style card assets go far higher: Jerabek's six-layer Chinese hairstyle is 46,221 triangles, Verhoolen's asset is 'about 40K polygons which is quite heavy for hair', and Lithvall's Aloy in Horizon Zero Dawn is 'a game mesh of 100k tris' driven by about 50 dynamic splines at 3 to 5 ms on PS4.

Three published ZBrush stylised-hair write-ups agree on getting the big hair shapes right before any detail, but only one describes the full chunk-flow-crevice-strand sequence. Munoz Gomez: create the initial volume (Standard Refiner or dam_Standard plus Move), identify the main "chunks" or "clumps" from reference, give the larger volumes "flow" with Surface Blocking, cut a "sharp crevice" pass with the Standard Blocking brush, then add thick strands with a CurveAlpha curve brush. Eder: review reference and break the hair into chunks, build each chunk from an IMM sphere with DynaMesh using Move, Smooth, Inflate and Pinch (ClayBuildup, DamStandard and TrimDynamic explicitly excluded), check shapes and silhouette against the concept, then lay DE_HairTubes strands over the temporary blockout; "Don't start detailing right away – take the time to get the basic shapes right!". He describes no flow or crevice step. Bazuichenko: a general volume of hair with DynaMesh, then polygon work with the Polish and Pinch brushes, following an Adam Fisher video; she does not mention chunks, flow, crevices or strands.
claims.as_first_reported: Published ZBrush stylised-hair workflows (Dan Eder, Pablo Munoz Gomez, Kristina Bazuichenko) all block the whole hair volume first, cut it into chunks matched to reference, give the chunks flow and crevices, and only then add strands; Eder blocks out with Move, Smooth, Inflate and Pinch only and defers detail until the big shapes read.

claims.claim: Dan Eder's Gnomon workshop states the shape rules for stylised hair as: prioritise directionality, variation and clean silhouettes; avoid wobbliness, repetitiveness and clumping; use varied strand sizes; keep polygon count low for flexibility; its chapters are Geometry, Curves and CurveAlpha, that is sculpted chunks, curve tubes and alpha strands.

claims.claim: Hair Tool for Blender (paid addon, parameters cited as reference design only) builds strands from a curve profile that is Flat (ribbons) or Round (tubes) with width and resolution, Strand Uplift and Strand Protrusion, drawing parameters Elevation distance, Elevation falloff, Embed Roots Depth and Align tilt to surface, and curl generation with Gravity where 0.5 is natural pull.

Hair Tool for Blender (paid, cited only) stores its UV layout as rectangular UV boxes (regions) on one texture and assigns each strand or card one box, either by hand or picked at random from the boxes the user selects (Set UV Region with shift-click, Auto UV, or the UV Region Distribute deformer, which can be masked); an Offset UV control can stretch the mapping toward root or tip. The Hair Tool 2 docs add a 'Random UV flip' addon preference that creates X-axis-mirrored copies of each box for random assignment; the Hair Tool 3/4 docs document only a Y (top/down) flip by pressing 'F' over a box. The Hair Tool 3/4 docs list the bake passes Diffuse, AO, Normal Map, Opacity Mask, Root Mask (black to white gradient from root to tip), Random ID, Random Parent, Flow Map, Direction Map and Depth, with a 'Texture channel mixing' node editor to pack baked maps into new RGBA channels; the Hair Tool 2 docs list Diffuse, AO, Normal Map, Opacity Mask, Root Mask, Random ID mask, Flow Map, Direction and Depth Mask, without Random Parent.
claims.as_first_reported: Hair Tool for Blender (paid, cited only) gives each card a straight rectangular UV over one atlas slot chosen at random from its group's UV boxes, optionally X-flipped, and bakes Diffuse, AO, Normal, Opacity Mask, Root Mask (black-to-white root to tip), Random ID, Random Parent, Flow Map, Direction Map and Depth passes with optional RGBA channel packing.

claims.claim: VRoid Studio builds anime hair as bundles drawn on a guide mesh around the head or generated procedurally with count, cross-section and twist parameters; its material gives each bundle a base texture plus a separate highlight texture, positioned per group or per strand, with texture Width defaulting to 1.8 (the last two per a user write-up).

Stylised hair in Blender is commonly built from NURBS curves with a bevel object as cross-section, and Blender 4.5's curve Geometry panel turns a curve into a ribbon with Extrude, scales it along its length with a Taper Object (Y=1 unchanged, Y=0.5 half) and into a tube with Bevel (Round, Object or Profile).

No primary Blizzard, Epic, Riot, Nintendo, miHoYo or Rare text on hair geometry construction, piece counts or texture sizes was found for Overwatch, Fortnite, Valorant, Zelda, Genshin or Sea of Thieves; Blizzard pages mention only ZBrush concept sculpts, Rare's lead character artist shows 'initial 3D sculpting style tests for the hair', and Zelda sources cover cel shading only.

A commercial stylised semi-realistic hair-card pack (11 short styles on ArtStation Marketplace) ships Albedo, Alpha, Specular, Normal, Direction, Height, Occlusion and Thickness maps, and Leti M. Vila and Mariia Zatorska both also use a root-to-tip gradient.

Tubes are the stylised primitive in both game and cinematic work: Leti M. Vila built each hair 'flake' separately with curve tubes, focusing only on big shapes and good flow, and Blizzard groom artist Becca Baldwin calls 'tube grooming', where each line of a modelled tube becomes an XGen curve, her preferred method for stylised characters.

Overwatch-style fan reconstructions use sculpted 'geometry hair' (ZBrush high poly, Maya low poly, hair on its own 2048x2048 texture set), and polycount feedback for the look is anisotropic rather than GGX reflection, alpha or dither at tips and roots, and a plain texture that lets the flow and specular maps do the work.

Stylised hair highlights are authored rather than simulated: Genshin Impact's painted anime shine marks and shadows double as the mask for a real-time specular (with a fake subsurface tint at shadow edges), Fortiche paints Arcane's highlights and shadows into textures, and Gabriel Lopes's Marmoset character drives Reflectivity and Clearcoat from specular maps holding highlights only where wanted.

The Unity Toon Shader 'Angel Ring' is a hair highlight fixed in screen space from the camera, driven by a hand-drawn texture on a second UV set projected orthographically from the character's front; Offset U ranges 0 to 0.5 (default 0), Offset V 0 to 1 (default 0.3), and the texture alpha can act as a clipping mask.

Arcane-style fan pipelines build hair as sculpted clumps (ZBrush CurveTube ropes refined with Move and HPolish), paint each clump a different colour with its own polygroup to read the flow, and one finished Arcane study character totals 64,158 tris with hair on its own 4K UDIM scalable to 1K.

Reallusion's CC Hair Creation Guide says to model the scalp first by copying portions of the base model head mesh and scaling them outwards to cover the base mesh. The CC 3.4 Hair Mesh Production page gives, as its suggested method, directly extracting the scalp mesh from the character's head, and adds that the mesh can also be created manually for special requirements. Only the Creation Guide mentions scaling outwards; neither page gives an offset distance or scale factor.
claims.as_first_reported: Reallusion's guides make the scalp mesh by copying or extracting the head's own scalp faces and scaling them outwards to sit just over the head, rather than modelling a fresh dome; neither page gives the offset amount.

claims.claim: Widening a card at its root is a deliberate way to cover the scalp without adding cards, and leaving scalp visible in the base layer is acceptable when a breakup layer will fill it.

The parting is a planning input rather than a card trick: Zatorska lists the parting's shape among the reference questions answered before any cards are placed, and Reallusion treats exposed scalp along a parting as needing baked follicles; no opened page gives a step-by-step for drawing the part line on the cap.

Unreal can generate a Follicle texture, a small distance field of the groom's strand roots projected into the head's UVs at a power-of-two size with a Root Radius in pixels, so the skin material itself darkens or roughens where hair grows; Epic's example packs hair, eyelashes and stubble into separate colour channels.

Unreal's groom LOD 'Meshes' type is a low-poly hair helmet supporting only RBF deformation, its Strands Textures (Depth, Coverage, Tangent, Attributes, Material) are generated by projecting strands onto that mesh, and MetaHuman grooms run up to 8 LODs with LOD 3 the highest card LOD.

VRoid Studio's hair editor draws hair on 'the guide mesh generated around the head' and lists a separate 'Base Hair' item that can only be renamed or toggled visible, so a bald look is made by hiding the base hair, not editing it.

In MakeHuman and MPFB, hair is an MHCLO clothes asset, 'a mesh object combined with instructions on how a vertex on the asset should be matched with a vertex on the Basemesh'; the bundled short02 hair, measured from the makehuman-py3-assets mirror on 2026-09-22, is a 1,755-vertex, 1,672-face OBJ with a 2048x2048 RGBA diffuse 57.9 percent fully transparent, rendered with alphaToCoverage.

The makehuman-py3-assets mirror of MakeHuman's bundled hair is licensed under the GNU Affero General Public License v3.0: its LICENSE file is the AGPLv3 text and its README says the assets are 'provided under the standard makehuman license (AGPL)', while also mentioning a 'CC0 exception used in releases' whose terms were not read.

claims.claim: Reallusion's CC 3.4 Hair Mesh Production guide (wiki, last modified 4 June 2021) says hair cards must originate from the scalp ("Do not float the hair cards in mid-air and do not insert the hair cards right into the scalp mesh"), advises trying to avoid many large hair cards to reduce a polygonal look while allowing some if the amount is considered, and recommends striving to divide the hair into three levels or more, roughly dense, abundant and sparse, with the base mostly dense and abundant and sparse cards layered on top.
claims.as_first_reported: Reallusion requires hair cards to originate at the scalp surface, neither floating above it nor inserted into the scalp mesh, and to avoid many large cards, organising them as three or more levels of dense, abundant and sparse cards.

Do not float the hair cards in mid-air and do not insert the hair cards right into the scalp mesh." Section "Hair Card Distribution": "Compared with the large hair cards with rough layout recommended by the old process, users should pay attention to realism and increased layering. Therefore, try to avoid using many large hair cards to reduce the polygonal look (jaggedness of the hair). [...] You can still use large hair cards that resemble those used in the old process, however, do consider the amount used." Section "Hair Card Layering": "As mentioned earlier, we should strive to increase the layering of the hair by dividing the hair into three levels or more. Roughly speaking, the three levels are: dense, abundant, and sparse hair. [...] One can tell that the base of the hair is comprised of mostly dense strands, while it is essential to layer abundant and sparse hair cards on top to achieve a layering effect." The section preamble frames all of this as guidance: "The following are some common mistakes made by developers and some points to pay attention to, in order to increase productivity."
checks.notes: Refuted only in part, on modality and scope, not on substance. Every name and number in the claim is on the page verbatim: scalp origin, no floating, no insertion into the scalp mesh, avoid many large cards, "three levels or more", "dense, abundant, and sparse". What the source does not support is the single verb "requires" governing all three points: the scalp rule is imperative ("make sure", "Do not"), but the large-card point is "try to avoid" with an explicit allowance for some large cards, and the levels point is "we should strive to", i.e. recommendations in a section the page itself calls "common mistakes ... and some points to pay attention to". The page is also specific to Character Creator 3.4 content development, which the claim drops. On the second source: the wiki's own "For next-generation visuals, see the works done by Naughty Dog: Artstation Link" points to https://www.artstation.com/artwork/Aq5VXy, not to 3oZZDo, so 3oZZDo is not the page the wiki cites; its content was not readable in this check (403 over curl, racy shared browser), so it neither supports nor contradicts the claim and should not be listed as a source for Reallusion's wording. Incidental: the browser race exposed a Mariia Zatorska blog page (https://marizatorska.artstation.com/blog/vq7Z/...) describing a "Hair Cap" mesh "placed under the hair cards" for short styles; that was not part of this check but is relevant to finding (e) "needs a scalp texture". Web search budget for this session was exhausted (200 of 200), so the artist of 3oZZDo was not identified. Corrected wording: Reallusion's CC 3.4 Hair Mesh Production guide (wiki, last modified 4 June 2021) says hair cards must originate from the scalp ("Do not float the hair cards in mid-air and do not insert the hair cards right into the scalp mesh"), advises trying to avoid many large hair cards to reduce a polygonal look while allowing some if the amount is considered, and recommends striving to divide the hair into three levels or more, roughly dense, abundant and sparse, with the base mostly dense and abundant and sparse cards layered on top.

claims.claim: In Reallusion's Character Creator pipeline the scalp and the strips are separate geometry with separate materials, 'hair_scalp' and 'hair_strips', both taking diffuse, bump, specular, opacity and RGB mask maps, with the strip material also taking a physics map.

Reallusion's newer Smart Hair process requires the scalp to carry the same six texture channels as the hair (base colour, opacity, flow, ID, root, depth), so cap and cards share a channel set even as separate materials.

Reallusion's scalp texture rules: the scalp diffuse is darker than the strip diffuse to read as occluded hair but not so dark that the hairline segments sharply, the scalp opacity map has slightly blurred edges to blend into the head, and the specular map carries the same black cut-out as the opacity map.
claims.as_first_reported: Reallusion's scalp texture rules: the scalp diffuse is darker than the strip diffuse to read as occluded hair but not so dark that the hairline segments sharply, the scalp opacity map has slightly blurred edges to blend into the head, and the specular map carries the same black cut-out as the opacity map.

claims.claim: Reallusion's CC 3.4 hair wiki splits scalp textures into two types, both headed "(Old Process)": "gap fillers", which fill empty or sparse areas of the hair, need only opacity and diffuse textures, reduce the hair geometry needed and soften the skin-to-hair transition (and, per the Introduction page, hand-painting in Photoshop remains acceptable for scalp textures that only demarcate the hairline); and "exposed scalp", which is viewed directly without being obstructed by hair and so needs clearly defined hair follicles, "not just color fills", and is suited to buzz cuts and areas of hair too intricate or elaborate for hair card placement. The page says most of the game industry obtains scalp textures by baking, and its exposed-scalp production process bakes an XGen Interactive Groom of hair cards to a low-poly mesh in xNormal, but it also says the old process can still give good results and leaves the choice to the Art Lead.
claims.as_first_reported: Reallusion splits scalp use into 'gap fillers', which only fill sparse areas under the cards, need only opacity and diffuse maps and may be hand-painted to mark the hairline, and 'exposed scalp' (buzz cuts, partings), which is seen directly and must show clearly defined, evenly distributed hair follicles, normally baked from strands, rather than colour fill.

checks.read: https://wiki.reallusion.com/Content_Dev:CC_3.4_Hair_Creation_Process ; https://wiki.reallusion.com/Content_Dev:CC_3.4_Hair_Creation_Introduction
checks.evidence: Process page, section "Brief Introduction to Baking Scalp Textures" > "Scalp Types", which has exactly two sub-headings, "Gap Fillers (Old Process)" and "Exposed Scalp (Old Process)". Gap Fillers: "The scalp can be used to fill in empty or sparse areas of the hair, and only the opacity and diffuse textures are required to fulfill this criteria. Proper scalp fills can reduce the amount of necessary hair geometry and the load on the system as a result. It can also help to create a natural look for the transition between the skin the hair. For this purpose, the older, and faster method for production is sufficient." Exposed Scalp: "The difference between gap fillers and exposed scalps, is that the exposed scalp can be viewed directly without being obstructed by the hair. Therefore, exposed scalp need to have clearly defined hair follicles -not just color fills. This is so that the visuals for the scalp can be adjusted for the new shader. Exposed scalp is suitable for buzz cuts and areas of hair that are too intricate or elaborate for hair card placement." Same section, preamble: "Although most of the game industry uses the baking process to obtain scalp textures, it does not mean that the old process will not have good visual results." "Exposed Scalp Production Process": "The baking process with xNormal is basically the same as the one mentioned above ... Use hair cards instead of hair tubes ... Use Xgen's Interactive Groom Editor because it's more suitable for shorter scalp hair." Introduction page, "Reasons Behind Relegating the Legacy Workflow": "Although it is not recommended to use hand-painting in Photoshop to complete hair textures, as suggested in this procedure, it can still be used for scalp textures that only serve to demarcate the hairline." NOT in source: the word "parting"/"partings" appears nowhere on either page (grep of the full page text for parting|part|parted returned nothing). "evenly distributed" is not in the scalp section; the only "distribute the hair follicles evenly" line is under "Texture Layout Concept" > "Additional Tips", a list of mock-up tips for hair CARD textures ("Distribution: do distribute the hair follicles evenly with variation coming from the way that the hair strands flow.").
checks.notes: Confirmed verbatim: the two-way split; "only the opacity and diffuse textures are required"; "viewed directly without being obstructed by the hair"; "clearly defined hair follicles -not just color fills"; "buzz cuts"; hand-painting kept for scalp textures that "only serve to demarcate the hairline" (Introduction page). (2) "evenly distributed" is borrowed from the hair-card texture layout tips, not from the exposed-scalp passage. (3) "normally baked from strands" is only loosely supported: the page says "most of the game industry uses the baking process to obtain scalp textures" and the exposed-scalp bake uses XGen groom hair cards (not tubes) in xNormal; the stronger line "baking is the only viable solution when it comes to producing scalp textures" sits under "Hair Bake Methodology", which is prefaced "The following is the opinion of the original author, and does not represent the views of Reallusion." Minor: "under the cards" is inferred; the source says "empty or sparse areas of the hair". Also worth recording: both scalp types are labelled "(Old Process)" in their headings, and the section's comparison table rates the old process as shorter, lower-resolution, better-performing and with "More" visual harmony but "No Support" for the new shader. claims.claim: Reallusion's scalp texture is built up in layers from a shaded fuzzy base, feathered and blurred, on an evenly laid-out scalp UV, with suggested map sizes of diffuse 128 to 512 px, specular, bump and opacity 256 to 1024 px, and RGB mask 8 to 256 px.

One documented way to make the cap texture is a bake: Zatorska (vq7Z, 2021, recreating Turk's workflow) grows hair with Maya's Interactive Grooming tool, converts it to "tiny splines" and bakes it onto a low-poly cap mesh in Marmoset Toolbag, yielding Alpha, Normal, Ambient Occlusion, Depth, Id and Root maps, and says xNormal or Blender can bake them as well; Turk says that once the groom is converted to geometry "any software can be used to bake", and shows the cap's texture sheets as a set separate from the card clump sheets. In her 2020 list of "a few ways to create the hair cap" (9BDv), Zatorska gives the bake as one option alongside painting in Substance Painter (her own way at the time), baking in ZBrush, and painting in ZBrush and Photoshop. Neither source calls the bake "standard", says the strands are short or grown on the cap, or says anything about the cap texture not being a copy of the card atlas roots.
claims.as_first_reported: The standard cap texture is a bake, not a copy of the card atlas roots: short strands are grown on the cap, converted to geometry and baked to the low-poly cap in Marmoset, xNormal or Blender, yielding Alpha, Normal, AO, Depth, ID and Root maps; Zatorska also lists painting in Substance Painter, ZBrush or Photoshop.

checks.evidence: Paper: Tojo, Hu, Umetani, Li, "Strands2Cards: Automatic Generation of Hair Cards from Strands", "In SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 Conference Papers (SA Conference Papers '25), December 15-18, 2025, Hong Kong", doi 10.1145/3757377.3763864. Section 3.1, "Detail-preserving strand alignment": "we generate textures by aligning the overall curved geometry of the strands into normalized UVW space while preserving high-frequency strand details (see Figure 4). Here, the W-axis is defined to be orthogonal to the UV plane." Fig. 4 caption: "We first compute the principal component analysis of the hair root points to define the UV coordinate axes in 3D. We smooth the input strand to make a smooth handle. We use linear blend skinning to straighten the overall strand geometry." Body: "For each wisp, we first rigidly rotate the strands using PCA so that their root positions exhibit minimal variation along the W-axis. ... We then apply a 2D rotation in the UV plane to align the projection of the guide strand's root-to-tip vector, u_L - u_1, with the negative V-axis." "Specifically, we employ a Gaussian kernel, eta_{l,k} = exp(-(||u_l u_k||/beta)^2), where ||u_l u_k|| is the arc-length distance between vertices, and the weights are normalized to sum to 1. In practice, beta typically ranges between 2 cm to 3 cm, with smaller values producing straighter aligned strands and larger values allowing more curvature." "We then compute the rough straightening transformation of the smoothed handle into a straight line, referred to as the target line, which is aligned with the negative V-axis while preserving its original arc length." "we deform the original 3D strands into their aligned poses {u-hat_l} via linear blend skinning (LBS) [Jacobson et al. 2014] as: u-hat_l = sum_k eta_{l,k} A_k u_k (1)". "After aligning all the strands within a wisp, we render the texture of the corresponding polygon strip using an orthographic camera oriented along the W-axis." Texture compression: representative textures "are tightly packed into 4096 x 4096 images". Fig. 2 caption: "we align each wisp in UVW space such that the strands approximately orient along the V-axis. We then fit polystrip meshes to the wisp shapes using differentiable rendering." Section 3.2: "we propose a method to robustly optimize curved strips"; "Each polygon strip is initialized around the guide strand of the corresponding wisp."
checks.notes: Every named element (SIGGRAPH Asia 2025, PCA on root points defining UV axes, guide strand root-to-tip vector to negative V, Gaussian kernel with beta 2 to 3 cm, LBS, straighten while preserving high-frequency detail, packed atlas) is stated in the PDF with those names and numbers. Three small precisions the register could carry: (1) the paper says beta "typically ranges between 2 cm to 3 cm", i.e. a typical range not a fixed setting, and explicitly says larger beta "allow[s] more curvature" to remain in the aligned strands, so the slot is a "rough straightening" of the handle-scale shape rather than strictly straight; (2) it is the projection of the guide strand's root-to-tip vector into the UV plane that is aligned to negative V, and PCA proper fixes the W axis (minimal root variance, sign chosen by the guide root tangent) with the in-plane rotation coming from the guide strand; (3) "so curvature lives in the card mesh" is the researcher's inference, not a sentence in the paper: the paper supports it by removing the "overall curved geometry" from the texture, initialising each strip around the curved guide strand and optimising "curved strips" to "fit polystrip meshes to the wisp shapes", but never writes that conclusion. Also worth knowing for the repo: the paper criticises UE5 HairCardGenerator for an "overly straight appearance" on dreadlocks because it drops fine-scale strand detail, so the intended reading is "straight at the wisp scale, detailed at the strand scale", which the claim's "while keeping high-frequency strand detail" already captures. The project page itself contains only the abstract ("skinning-based alignment of the strands into a normalized pose in UV space"); all numbers come from the PDF. Optional tighter wording: "... linear blend skinning with Gaussian kernel weights (beta typically 2 to 3 cm; smaller is straighter, larger keeps more curvature) maps each strand's smoothed handle onto a straight line along negative V while keeping high-frequency strand detail; the wisp-scale curvature is then carried by the curved strip mesh initialised around the guide strand and fitted by differentiable rendering."

The claim does not rest on a single blog post: Unity docs, FiberShop docs, Izdebski, Haines and NVIDIA agree. Corrected wording: Colour under transparent texels should be dilated past the alpha edge (or the texture premultiplied), because mipmap generation averages the RGB of discarded texels into the edge and runtime bilinear sampling interpolates between an opaque texel and its transparent neighbour, both pulling the hidden colour into strand edges: Unity's 'Alpha is Transparency' import option dilates the colour channels, and FiberShop's 'export advanced' mode warns that PNG alpha is treated as a transparency mask so 'transparent pixels will be removed from all channels', recommending TGA when packing a map into alpha.

claims.claim: Box-filtered alpha mips lower alpha-test coverage at every level so cards thin and vanish with distance; Castano's fix in NVIDIA Texture Tools measures coverage = Sum(a_i > A_r)/N on the base level, bisects a per-mip reference a_r giving equal coverage and scales alpha by A_r / a_r, which Unity exposes as 'Preserve Coverage' with 'Alpha Cutoff'.

Funcom's Conan Exiles guide bakes Fibermesh hair in xNormal with padding 1 and anti-aliasing 2x for tests and 4x for final, at twice the intended in-game resolution then scaled down 50%, with Fibermesh profile at least 4 and 30+ segments for long hair, packing base colour, root mask, height and opacity into one _D texture and colour ID into _Shift.

Hossimo's XGen workflow renders a 4096x4096 orthographic front view with a directional light, primitive width about 0.35 in scene units with a width ramp tapering the tip thinner than the root, length randomised as $a * rand(0.8,1.2), then broad and subtle clumping modifiers, a cut modifier, noise and optionally coil.

lisyarus's comparison of nine alpha-mip methods on foliage found coverage-preserving remapping 'pretty similar to simple averaging', max-downsampled signed-distance-field alpha 'works stunningly well' but leaks colour, and premultiplied colour plus SDF alpha 'works perfectly' yet breaks packed atlases because SDFs leak between neighbouring slots.

Wyman and McGuire (NVIDIA, I3D 2017) show alpha-tested geometry erodes with distance (a 5 px wire thins to about 1 px then vanishes), their example hair texture averages alpha 0.32 'partly due to artist-added padding' so coarse mips fail the test, and hashed alpha testing replaces the fixed threshold with a stable per-pixel hash to keep coverage.

Strands2Cards renders per-wisp opacity, tangent, depth and strand-index maps from strands as constant-radius tubes under an orthographic camera, packs representative wisps into 4096x4096 images sorted by bounding-box height, shares 20 compressed textures across 200 to 300 k-means clusters, and sub-samples strands at 1/2 to 1/4 to stop opacity maps saturating.

Godot's StandardMaterial3D docs say Alpha Hash 'is suited for realistic-looking hair, although stylized hair may work better with alpha scissor', Alpha Scissor discards below a threshold while Alpha Hash dithers, the Alpha Edge Blend and Alpha Edge Clip antialiasing modes need MSAA 3D of at least 2x, and Depth Pre-Pass draws fully opaque pixels first.

Reallusion's CC 3.4 hair shader takes Opacity (Gaussian filtering, no padding), Z-depth, Flow, ID, Root and AO ('closest' filtering with edge padding) plus optional Base Color, with padding 32 px minimum, strands 2 px wide or more, UV islands 10 to 20 px apart, and 4K square output (2048x4096 allowed for long hair).

Blender 4.5's Data Transfer modifier copies Custom Normals as Face Corner Data (bpy: use_loop_data=True, data_types_loops={'CUSTOM_NORMAL'}; loop_mapping default 'NEAREST_POLYNOR'; mix_mode default 'REPLACE'). The API reference prints the modifier's mix_factor RNA default as 0.0 and the operator bpy.ops.object.data_transfer defaults mix_factor to 1.0, but a modifier created with obj.modifiers.new(..., 'DATA_TRANSFER') is initialised to mix_factor 1.0 (measured in Blender 4.5.9 LTS; MOD_datatransfer.cc init_data sets it to 1.0f), so setting mix_factor=1.0 explicitly is harmless but not required. data_types_loops does have to be set explicitly: a new modifier has an empty set even though the API page prints "default {'CUSTOM_NORMAL'}" (measured).

checks.notes: What the sources support exactly: the property names, the enum identifiers CUSTOM_NORMAL and NEAREST_POLYNOR, the defaults 'NEAREST_POLYNOR' and 'REPLACE', the API's printed "default 0.0" for the modifier's mix_factor, and the operator's mix_factor=1.0. What fails: the conclusion "so a script must set mix_factor=1.0 explicitly". The 0.0 in the API reference is the RNA-declared default (what bl_rna reports and what a reset-to-default would use), not the value a new modifier gets; modifiers.new() runs the modifier's init_data, which sets 1.0f. A script that omits mix_factor therefore already transfers at full strength. Two smaller points. (1) The API page's "default {'CUSTOM_NORMAL'}" for data_types_loops is a documentation artefact of the flag enum (RNA default is 0 in rna_modifier.cc line 7339); measured, both the RNA default and a new modifier's value are the empty set, so the claim's advice to set data_types_loops={'CUSTOM_NORMAL'} is right, but the researcher's quoted evidence for that default is not a real default. (2) The manual lists Custom Normals under "Data Types" as a toggle button, not under a heading called "Face Corner Data"; its "Face Corner Data" terms sit in the Mapping section (e.g. "Nearest Corner and Best Matching Face Normal"). The grouping the claim describes comes from the RNA labels, measured as use_loop_data name "Face Corner Data" and data_types_loops name "Face Corner Data Types". Neither point changes the verdict on its own; the mix_factor conclusion does. checks.notes: Lens finding: the claim conflates two different "defaults" in Blender, the RNA property default (what the API doc generator prints from bl_rna, and what bpy.types.X.bl_rna.properties[...].default returns) and the DNA struct default (what a newly added modifier actually holds). For DataTransfer these disagree in both directions: mix_factor RNA 0.0 vs DNA 1.0; data_types_loops RNA {'CUSTOM_NORMAL'} vs DNA 0 (empty set). The researcher's doc reading is accurate; only the inference drawn from it is wrong, and it was "read, not run". The three cited docs.blender.org URLs are currently behind a Cloudflare challenge for non-browser clients (HTTP 403 with a "Just a moment..." body from both WebFetch and curl with a browser UA), so the pages were verified through a Wayback snapshot dated 2026-03-09 and the manual's RST source on projects.blender.org; the claim does not rest on a single blog or forum post, the second independent source is the tagged Blender source and a live run. Not checked: whether the docs.blender.org 4.5 page text has changed since the 2026-03-09 snapshot (unlikely to matter, the RNA definition at tag v4.5.9 is what the generator reads). Version drift note for the register: in Blender 4.0 and earlier, custom-normal transfer also required the destination mesh's Auto Smooth to be on; that requirement is gone in 4.1+ and did not surface in the 4.5.9 run (no modifier error, has_custom_normals=True on the result). Corrected wording: Blender 4.5's Data Transfer modifier copies Custom Normals as Face Corner Data (bpy: use_loop_data=True, data_types_loops={'CUSTOM_NORMAL'}; loop_mapping default 'NEAREST_POLYNOR'; mix_mode default 'REPLACE'). The API reference lists the modifier property's RNA default as mix_factor 0.0 while the bpy.ops.object.data_transfer operator defaults to 1.0, but a modifier created in a script (ob.modifiers.new or bpy.ops.object.modifier_add) starts at mix_factor = 1.0 from Blender's DNA defaults, so custom normals transfer in full without setting it; setting mix_factor=1.0 explicitly is harmless but not required. What a script must set is use_loop_data=True and data_types_loops={'CUSTOM_NORMAL'}: a new modifier holds data_types_loops = set() despite the reference listing {'CUSTOM_NORMAL'} as the enum's default. (Source at tag v4.5.9 read; behaviour run in Blender 4.5.9 LTS on 2026-09-22.)

claims.claim: Since Blender 4.1 use_auto_smooth is removed, meshes always use custom normals if they exist and MeshLoop.normal is read-only; Shade Smooth by Angle (bpy.ops.object.shade_smooth_by_angle, angle=0.523599) and Mesh.set_sharp_from_angle fill the sharp_edge attribute but are not required for custom normals, which take precedence whenever present.

Unity HDRP's hair documentation states 'If you use semi-transparent hair cards, you must manually sort them so that they are in back-to-front order from every viewing direction', and recommends cards for secondary characters and lower levels of detail, with strands only for main characters.

In Blender 4.5 the Principled BSDF's Anisotropic, Anisotropic Rotation and Tangent inputs are marked 'Cycles Only' and the Principled Hair BSDF is 'Cycles Only', so under EEVEE a Principled BSDF on hair cards is an isotropic specular with no strand-direction highlight.

Since Blender 4.2 EEVEE's Blend Mode is replaced by Render Method: Dithered (the former Alpha Hashed, compatible with render passes and raytracing) and Blended (the former Alpha Blend), Alpha Clip is reproduced with a Math Greater Than node, and Blended sorts per object by origin only, since 'EEVEE does not support per-fragment (pixel) sorting or per-triangle sorting'.

claims.claim: Cycles caps transparent bounces separately from other bounces (Transparent Max Bounces: min 0, max 1024, default 8, per intern/cycles/blender/addon/properties.py; the 4.5 manual says only that the count is 'controlled separately from other bounces' and gives no numbers). scene/integrator.cpp passes the UI value plus one to the kernel, and path_state.h raises PATH_RAY_TERMINATE_ON_NEXT_SURFACE once the path's transparent-bounce counter reaches that kernel cap, so at the default 8 the flag is set after the ninth transparent pass and the tenth surface along the ray ends the path: its holdout and emission are still written, but it gets no direct light and no further bounce, so a tenth overlapping non-emissive alpha card contributes black. A material's Transparent Shadows option (Material.use_transparent_shadow in 4.2+, exposed in the material Settings panel) must be enabled for a card with a Transparent BSDF (including Principled alpha) to cast a cut-out shadow: without it the shader lacks SD_HAS_TRANSPARENT_SHADOW and the shadow-ray traversal treats the hit as fully blocking. Issues 120762 (closed 2024-05-07, resolved) and 124449 (closed 2024-07-12, archived after being linked to 120762) record hair-card and glass shadows ignoring alpha because that option was off after the 4.1 migration or in files saved from 4.1.

(b) Version drift on the option's location: the 4.5 Cycles addon properties.py contains no transparent_shadow property at all; the option is now the shared Material.use_transparent_shadow (RNA), which Cycles reads directly. The 4.5 manual source still labels it with the stale anchor `bpy.types.CyclesMaterialSettings.use_transparent_shadow`, so a reader following the manual's anchor would reach an attribute that no longer exists in 4.5; the claim's neutral wording "a material's Transparent Shadows option" avoids this. The 4.2 EEVEE release notes only mention adding a `Transparent Shadows` option for EEVEE; the unification commit named in 120762 is 6d0b5e2ace (4.1), read and not run. (c) "closed 2024-07-12 as duplicate": there is no Duplicate label; the issue carries Status/Archived and was closed by the reporter after the triager wrote "likely the same issue as #120762". Effectively a duplicate closure, but not a formal one. (d) Two nuances on "contributes black": emission is still written on the terminating surface, and in 4.5 a Ray Portal BSDF pass (LABEL_RAY_PORTAL) increments the same transparent counter; also min_transparent_bounces (default 0) enables probabilistic, throughput-weighted termination of transparent paths before the cap, so some paths can end earlier than the ninth card without bias. (e) The claim itself flags "Black-mass link untested"; nothing here tests whether the observed black mass in the repo's renders came from the cap (default 8) rather than from the finding (d) layering density; both remain plausible and a render with transparent_max_bounces raised to 32 or 64 would separate them. (f) Second independent source: the web search budget for this session was exhausted (200/200) so no forum or tutorial corroboration was gathered; the kernel code, RNA source and manual source are three independent primary files that agree, which is stronger than a forum answer. Corrected wording: Cycles counts transparent bounces separately from other bounces (Transparent Max Bounces: min 0, max 1024, default 8; read and not run, 4.5 release branch). When the counter reaches the cap, path_state_next sets PATH_RAY_TERMINATE_ON_NEXT_SURFACE and the next surface hit is shaded for holdout and emission only, then terminated, so with the default the ninth overlapping surface along a camera path adds nothing beyond its own emission (black for a non-emissive card); shadow rays share the same cap. Cut-out shadows through alpha require the material's Transparent Shadows option (bpy.types.Material.use_transparent_shadow since 4.1/4.2; it is no longer a material.cycles property); with it off the shader loses SD_HAS_TRANSPARENT_SHADOW and any hit blocks all light. claims.claim: Alpha to coverage converts fragment alpha into an MSAA coverage mask, so cards need no sorting but get only sampleCount+1 opacity levels (5 at 4x MSAA) and fall back to plain alpha test without MSAA; Golus sharpens the alpha to one pixel with col.a = (col.a - _Cutoff) / max(fwidth(col.a), 0.0001) + 0.5 and rescales alpha by mip level.

NVIDIA's Stochastic Transparency (Enderton et al., I3D 2010) names hair, with per-pixel depth complexity in the hundreds, as the motivating order-independent case, combining screen-door transparency, multi-sampling and random masks in one pass with one MSAA z-buffer and the same trick for shadow maps; by description EEVEE's Dithered (hashed) method is the same family.

The real-time card scheme is two-part alpha: Scheuermann (GDC 2004) alpha-tests the opaque cores, then draws transparent back faces, then front faces, in a static inside-to-outside index-buffer order sorted per connected patch, with an alpha texture that 'should have fully opaque regions'; Wronski does an alpha-tested pass with the reference alpha near 1.0 plus a blended pass for the rest.

For a head with hair this is very similar to inside to outside. Use static index buffer with inside to outside draw order, computed at preprocess time – Sort connected components (hair strand patches) instead of individual triangles". Slide 15 "Sorted Hair Rendering Scheme": "Pass 1 – opaque parts – Enable alpha test to only pass opaque pixels – Disable backface culling – Enable Z writes, set Z test to Less. Pass 2 – transparent back-facing parts – Enable alpha test to pass all non-opaque pixels – Cull front-facing polygons – Disable Z writes, set Z test to Less. Pass 3 – transparent front-facing parts – Enable alpha test to pass all non-opaque pixels – Cull back-facing polygons – Enable Z writes, set Z test to Less". Wronski, "Hair rendering trick(s)", 20 July 2014, step 1: "Render your hair with full specular occlusion / zero specularity. Do alpha testing in your shaders with value Aref close to 1.0. (Artist tweakable)."; step 4: "Render forward pass of hair specular and albedo for hair transparent part with alpha blending (scaled from 0 to Aref to 0-1 range), inverse alpha test (1-Aref) and regular depth test."; author's 2020 comment reply: "Valuable and still relevant is doing the alpha test and inverse alpha test trick with hair split as opaque vs transparent."
checks.notes: Every named element of the claim is in the sources: GDC 2004, three passes in the stated order (alpha-tested opaque, transparent back faces, transparent front faces), static preprocessed index buffer, inside-to-outside order, sorting by connected component (hair strand patch) rather than triangle, the quoted "should have fully opaque regions", Wronski's Aref close to 1.0, and a separate alpha-blended pass for the transparent remainder with inverse alpha test. Minor wording notes that do not change the verdict: (1) "opaque cores" is the claim's paraphrase; Scheuermann says "opaque parts" / "opaque pixels". (2) Neither source uses the word "card" (pdftotext grep for "card" returns 0 hits); Scheuermann says "polygonal hair model", "patches" and "hair strand patches", Wronski says "hair alpha tested stripes". (3) Wronski's full scheme is four steps: the alpha-tested pass at Aref is his G-buffer pass (step 1), then deferred lighting (step 2), then a forward specular pass that repeats the same alpha test with Z test set to equal (step 3), then the blended pass (step 4); the claim's "an alpha-tested pass plus a blended pass" compresses steps 1 and 3 into one, which matches the author's own summary "hair split as opaque vs transparent" but understates the pass count. (4) Scheuermann also gives an "Optimized Rendering Scheme" (slide 17) with four passes, adding a Z-buffer priming pass with colour writes disabled so early Z can replace the alpha test; the claim describes only the basic three-pass scheme. (5) Scheuermann's own caveat (slide 19): the sorting scheme "assumes little animation in hair model", dangling pony tails need separate handling, and it is "Not suitable for all hair styles".
