claims.claim: Unreal's Hair shading model exposes a Pixel Depth Offset input, which practitioners use to hide the visible lines where hair cards intersect each other and the scalp, and Unity HDRP's Hair stack has an equivalent Depth Offset block.

Cycles can bake ambient occlusion into a mesh colour attribute without a UV map: Bake Type 'Ambient Occlusion' ('Ignores all lights in the scene') with Output Target 'Active Color Attribute', and Fast GI Approximation's AO Distance can be overridden per object; baking to an image needs a UV map.

Mesh.normals_split_custom_set(normals) takes exactly one 3-vector per face corner (the RNA source reports 'Number of custom normals is not number of loops' otherwise), normals_split_custom_set_from_vertices takes one per vertex, zero vectors keep the automatic normal, and Mesh.has_custom_normals plus the read-only Mesh.corner_normals collection expose the result.

Cycles' shadow terminator controls are per object under Object Properties > Shading: Geometry Offset (object.cycles.shadow_terminator_geometry_offset, default 0.1, affecting only triangles at grazing angles to the light, the preferred fix) and Shading Offset (object.cycles.shadow_terminator_offset, default 0.0, which 'is not energy conserving').

The Data Transfer modifier's custom-normals path regressed in the Blender 4.0 alpha (issue 111898, reported 2023-09-03 as 'often doesn't work or produces incorrect results', caused by commit 5e9ea9243b33) and was resolved on 2023-09-06, so older forum reports of the modifier 'not working' do not apply to 4.5.

Blender 4.5's C++ OBJ importer (source/blender/io/wavefront_obj/importer/, C++ since commit e6a9b22384 of 2022-04-04) turns per-corner 'vn' references into custom normals through bke::mesh_set_custom_normals (stored in 4.5 as a CORNER INT16_2D "custom_normal" attribute), and when the file has any 'vn' data it sets no face sharpness from 's' lines (only degenerate faces with area below 1e-12 are marked sharp); this is decided per file, not per object, because has_normals() checks the file's global normal list. With no 'vn' data at all, 's off' sets sharp_face true. For an MTL map_d image it links the Image Texture node's Alpha output into the Principled BSDF Alpha socket and sets the MA_BL_HIDE_BACKFACE flag (bpy: use_transparency_overlap and show_transparent_back become False). It also writes the legacy DNA field blend_method = MA_BM_BLEND, but in Blender 4.2 and later that field is deprecated and unread by EEVEE: the importer leaves surface_render_method at its default, so the material renders as Dithered (not Blended, the successor of Alpha Blend) and bpy reports blend_method 'HASHED' and surface_render_method 'DITHERED' (measured, 4.5.9). Cycles, which this repo renders with, ignores both fields and honours the Alpha socket link. The MTL colour's alpha is never read: Base Color alpha is forced to 1.0; the scalar 'd' line is read separately into the Alpha socket's default value.
claims.as_first_reported: Blender 4.5's C++ OBJ importer turns per-corner 'vn' references into custom normals through bke::mesh_set_custom_normals, setting no face sharpness from 's' lines when normals exist, and wires an MTL map_d image's Alpha output into the Principled BSDF Alpha socket while switching the material to Alpha Blend with backface hiding; the colour's alpha is not read from the MTL.

checks.notes: All four sub-claims hold against the v4.5 release source, read and not run. Three precision points for anyone reusing the claim. (1) The final sentence is a trap if paraphrased: what is "not read from the MTL" is only the fourth component of RGBA socket values (Base Color, Emission Color), which set_property_of_socket hard-sets to 1.0. The MTL scalar `d` IS read (file_reader 905-906 into material->alpha) and, when != -1, is written to the Principled "Alpha" float socket (obj_import_mtl.cc 339-341); when d is in [0,1) or the illum mode implies transparency, the material is also switched to MA_BM_BLEND with MA_BL_HIDE_BACKFACE (342-345). So "the colour's alpha is not read" is right; "the MTL's alpha is not read" would be wrong. (2) "Setting no face sharpness from 's' lines when normals exist" is exact, but there is one non-'s' exception: degenerate faces with area < 1e-12 are still marked sharp (mesh.cc 262-273). (3) has_normals() is file-global: any `vn` in the file plus a non-empty corner count disables 's'-based sharpness for that mesh, and a corner with no `vn` index (or an out-of-range one) gets a (0,0,0) custom normal (mesh.cc 417-421), not a computed one. Also: "Alpha Blend" and "backface hiding" are the claim's names for MA_BM_BLEND and MA_BL_HIDE_BACKFACE; the source uses the constants, not those labels. The cited manual HTML could not be opened (Cloudflare 403); its RST source was read and says only that a matching .MTL's materials are imported, nothing on normals, sharpness or alpha, so the claim rests entirely on the two .cc files, which is appropriate.

Since the 4.2 EEVEE rewrite the DNA blend_method field is a forward-compatibility leftover (rna_material.cc line 222 "Still sets the legacy property for forward compatibility"), so the importer's write changes nothing a 4.5 user or script can see except when the .blend is later opened in a pre-4.2 Blender. The backface-hiding half of that clause does hold in 4.5: eevee_pipeline.cc line 401 reads MA_BL_HIDE_BACKFACE in ForwardPipeline::prepass_transparent_add, but only for the forward (Blended) pipeline, which the importer does not enable. Practical consequence for this repo: irrelevant to Cycles renders; relevant if anyone expects EEVEE or the viewport to blend the hair cards after OBJ import, they will be dithered instead. Source stability: the same lines exist unchanged in the main branch on 2026-09-22 (main obj_import_mtl.cc lines 407 to 409 and obj_import_mesh.cc lines 235 and 460; diff against 4.5 is includes, namespaces and image loading only). A side finding worth carrying into HAIR-080's register: because has_normals() is per file, an OBJ that mixes objects with and without 'vn' loses 's' handling for all of them (measured: the vn-less object in the mixed file got sharp_face [false,false] and a zero custom normal that resolves to the auto normal). Corrected wording: Blender 4.5's C++ OBJ importer (source/blender/io/wavefront_obj/importer/, C++ since commit e6a9b22384 of 2022-04-04) turns per-corner 'vn' references into custom normals through bke::mesh_set_custom_normals (stored in 4.5 as a CORNER INT16_2D "custom_normal" attribute), and when the file has any 'vn' data it sets no face sharpness from 's' lines (only degenerate faces with area below 1e-12 are marked sharp); this is decided per file, not per object, because has_normals() checks the file's global normal list. With no 'vn' data at all, 's off' sets sharp_face true. For an MTL map_d image it links the Image Texture node's Alpha output into the Principled BSDF Alpha socket and sets the MA_BL_HIDE_BACKFACE flag (bpy: use_transparency_overlap and show_transparent_back become False). It also writes the legacy DNA field blend_method = MA_BM_BLEND, but in Blender 4.2 and later that field is deprecated and unread by EEVEE: the importer leaves surface_render_method at its default, so the material renders as Dithered (not Blended, the successor of Alpha Blend) and bpy reports blend_method 'HASHED' and surface_render_method 'DITHERED' (measured, 4.5.9). Cycles, which this repo renders with, ignores both fields and honours the Alpha socket link. The MTL colour's alpha is never read: Base Color alpha is forced to 1.0; the scalar 'd' line is read separately into the Alpha socket's default value.

claims.claim: Epic's 2016 physically based hair shading (Karis) authors no normal, using a 'fake normal' and PCF shadow maps with exponential falloff, and reports 'little extra benefit from an authored normal when filtered shadowing was applied', the result being 'volumetric looking without any provided normals'.

Kajiya-Kay (1989) lights hair by the strand tangent T instead of a normal: diffuse K_d sin(T,L) and specular k_s ((T.L)(T.E) + sin(T,L) sin(T,E))^p, a Phong reflection cone about the tangent that uses the light and eye vectors, not a half vector. Scheuermann's GDC 2004 card shader (ATI Research, "Hair Rendering and Shading") recasts that specular as a half-angle term sin(T,H)^n = (1 - dot(T,H)^2)^(n/2), multiplies it by dirAtten = smoothstep(-1.0, 0.0, dot(T,H)), evaluates it twice on tangents shifted by normalize(T + shift * N) with different colours, exponents and shifts (the second masked by a noise texture), replaces the diffuse with saturate(lerp(0.25, 1.0, dot(N,L))) because the "Kajiya-Kay diffuse term sin(T, L) looks too bright without proper self-shadowing", and multiplies the result by a per-vertex ambient occlusion term (o.rgb *= ambOcc).
claims.as_first_reported: Kajiya-Kay lights hair by the strand tangent T, specular sin(T,H)^n, and Scheuermann's GDC 2004 card shader adds a smoothstep(-1, 0, dot(T,H)) attenuation, two highlights on tangents shifted by normalize(T + shift * N), a diffuse lerp(0.25, 1.0, N.L) because sin(T,L) 'looks too bright without proper self-shadowing', and a per-vertex ambient occlusion multiplier.

claims.claim: Marschner et al. (SIGGRAPH 2003) model a hair fibre as a transparent elliptical cylinder with absorbing interior and tilted cuticle scales, giving R, TT and TRT lobes with eta 1.55, alpha_R of -10 to -5 degrees and beta_R 5 to 10 degrees, and state Kajiya-Kay 'is not energy conserving' and ignores transmission and internal reflection.

Unreal's Hair shading model, a Marschner-style sum of R, TT and TRT lobes per Karis, exposes Base Color, Scatter, Specular, Roughness, Tangent, Backlit, Ambient Occlusion and Pixel Depth Offset, and its groom-to-cards pipeline expects Depth, Coverage, Tangent, Attributes (RootUV/CoordU/Seed), Material (Color/Roughness) and optional Auxiliary card textures.

Unity HDRP's Hair master stack offers Approximate (Kajiya-Kay based, cards only, tuned per lighting setup, described in HDRP 17 as 'an improved Kajiya Kay lighting model' for stylised looks) and Physical (Marschner based, energy conserving, multiple scattering only with strands), with blocks including Hair Strand Direction, Specular Shift, Secondary Specular Shift, Transmittance, Ambient Occlusion, Alpha Clip Threshold and Depth Offset.

Strands2Cards (SIGGRAPH Asia 2025, DOI 10.1145/3757377.3763864) converts strands to cards by k-means wisp clustering, per-wisp texture generation and strip fitting by differentiable rendering; Table 1 converts a 106K-strand model to 30K triangles in 1.6 s clustering, 6.1 s texture and 6.8 s fitting on an RTX 4090, and demo models use 200 to 300 strips with 20 compressed textures.

Strands2Cards (Tojo, Hu, Umetani, Li; SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 Conference Papers) k-means clusters strands on a feature vector that concatenates root position with a PCA projection of the remaining vertices (strands resampled to L = 100 vertices, centre of mass moved to the origin, subspace L' = 16). The cluster count sets the number of polygon strips, and the user chooses it to suit their polygon budget; typical values are 100 to 500. The paper's teaser and overview figures (Figure 1(b), Figure 2) use |M| = 300, which is also the default of --num_clusters in 1_cluster.py, but the real-time UE5 demo (Figure 1(c)) uses |M| = 200. Within each cluster, strands whose root's nearest-neighbour distance exceeds twice the average are dropped as statistical outliers (the code uses 5 neighbours, ratio 2.0), and each wisp's longest strand becomes its guide strand.

checks.evidence: Paper (Tojo, Hu, Umetani, Li, "Strands2Cards: Automatic Generation of Hair Cards from Strands", SA Conference Papers '25, December 15-18, 2025, Hong Kong, https://doi.org/10.1145/3757377.3763864), Section 3.1 "Wisp generation", verbatim: "Strand clustering. We first cluster input strand polylines S. Inspired by [Wang et al. 2009], we perform k-means clustering using the L2 distance between strand feature vectors as the metric. Prior to clustering, we resample strands to a uniform vertex count L = 100 and translate their center of mass to the origin. The feature vector for each strand S_s is then defined by concatenating its root position u1 and a low-dimensional projection u' in R^{L'} of the remaining vertex positions u = [u2, ..., uL] in R^{3(L-1)} computed via principal component analysis (PCA). The resulting feature vector is defined as [u1, u'] in R^{3+L'}. A small subspace dimension L' is desirable for efficient computation, and we found that a significantly reduced L' = 16 still produces high-quality wisps. The number of clusters determines the number of polygon strips |M| fitted to the resulting wisps. In this work, we allow users to specify the cluster count based on their desired polygon budget. Typical values range from 100 to 500 (see Figure 3), sufficiently preserving the hairstyle while significantly reducing geometric complexity compared to the original strands. With a small cluster count, the resulting wisps occasionally contain outlier strands that may disrupt texture rendering and strip computation. We remove these strands using statistical outlier filtering [Rusu et al. 2007] applied to strand root positions, identifying points whose nearest-neighbor distance exceeds twice the average as outliers. Guide strand selection. After clustering, we select the longest strand within each wisp as its guide strand." Code, 1_cluster.py (read verbatim): NUM_SAMPLES_PER_STRAND = 100; s2c.compute_strand_features(strands_np, n_components=16); s2c.cluster_points_kmeans(points=features, num_clusters=args.num_clusters); per cluster: root_points = cluster_strands[:, 0, :]; keep_mask = s2c.statistical_outlier_mask(root_points, n_neighbors=5, ratio=2.0); guide = first index per cluster in np.argsort(-lengths); parser default --num_clusters 300 ("Number of clusters (wisps)"). 2_texture.py: --config default "cluster300"; --num_quads default 15_000 ("Number of quad faces").
checks.notes: Every element of the claim is supported by the primary paper text, and the released code agrees on L = 100, 16 PCA components, root-position outlier filtering with ratio 2.0, and longest-strand guides. Three precision notes, none of which refute the claim: (1) "300 in the demo" comes from the released code defaults (--num_clusters 300 in 1_cluster.py, --config cluster300 in 2_texture.py), not from the paper text; the paper gives only the 100 to 500 range and Figure 3, whose count labels are rasterised in the PDF and could not be read. (2) "takes the cluster count as the polygon budget" is a slight compression: the paper says the cluster count determines the number of polygon strips |M| and the user picks it "based on their desired polygon budget"; the code has a separate quad budget (--num_quads, default 15,000) that allocates vertices along the strips proportionally to guide length, so cluster count = card count, and the polygon count is a second knob. (3) The outlier filter in code is a Rusu-style statistical filter over n_neighbors=5 with ratio 2.0, applied per cluster; the paper's "nearest-neighbor distance exceeds twice the average" is the authors' own summary of it. Conflation check: the paper uses PCA twice (feature projection for clustering, and a separate PCA of root points to define UVW axes in the alignment step, Fig. 4); the claim correctly refers to the clustering one. No predecessor/product drift found; paper, project page, and code are all by the same authors and consistent. Second independent source: this session's web search budget was exhausted (200 of 200) so no search could be run, and the ACM DL landing page returned 403; the claim therefore rests on the authors' primary sources only, which is appropriate for a paper-content claim. No third-party write-up was checked. The GitHub README states no licence (per the fetch summary; not read verbatim), so anything about reusing the code is a separate question.

checks.evidence: blender.org/about/license, verbatim: "The source code we develop at blender.org is default being licensed as GNU GPL Version 2 or later." ... "All the components that together make Blender are compatible under the newer GNU GPL Version 3 or later. That is also the license to use for any distribution of Blender binaries." Add-ons section: "Blender's Python API is an integral part of the software, used to define the user interface or develop tools for example. The GNU GPL license therefore requires that such scripts (if published) are being shared under a GPL compliant license. You are free to sell such scripts, but the sales then is restricted to the download service itself." Your Artwork section: "What you create with Blender is your sole property. All your artwork – images or movie files – including the .blend files and other data files Blender can write, is free for you to use as you like. That means that Blender can be used commercially by artists, by studios to make animation films or VFX, by game artists to work on commercial games, by scientists for research, and by students in educational institutions." FAQ (blender.org/support/faq): "Can I license .blend files myself? Yes. The output of Blender, in the form of .blend files, is considered program output, and the sole copyright of the user. The .blend file format only stores data definitions." and "What about add-ons or my Python scripts? If you share or publish Python scripts they have to be made available licensed as GNU GPL as well, if they use Blender Python API calls." GPLv3 as shipped in Blender's doc/license/GPL3-license.txt, section 2: "The output from running a covered work is covered by this License only if the output, given its content, constitutes a covered work." GPLv2 as shipped in doc/license/GPL-license.txt, section 0: "the output from the Program is covered only if its contents constitute a work based on the Program (independent of having been made by running the Program)." Bundled node groups: blender-assets repo LICENSE file is "CC0 1.0 Universal"; its README says bundled assets carry "License: 'CC0 - Public Domain'"; measured in the container, Blender 4.5.9 LTS, all 26 node groups with asset metadata in procedural_hair_node_assets.blend (e.g. 'Attach Hair Curves to Surface', 'Blend Hair Curves', 'Braid Hair Curves') report license='CC0 - Public Domain', copyright='Blender Foundation'.
checks.notes: Every quoted clause in the claim is on the licence page verbatim. The claim's inference (geometry produced by running Blender may ship in a game) is what the page itself says ("free for you to use as you like", "game artists to work on commercial games") and what both GPL texts say about program output; it does not go beyond the text. Two precision points, neither a refutation: (1) the page's script rule is scoped to scripts that use Blender's Python API and are published ("such scripts (if published)"; FAQ: "if they use Blender Python API calls"), and the FAQ says internal-only modified Blender or scripts need not be shared, so a tighter wording is "Python scripts and add-ons that use the bpy API must, if published or distributed, be shared under a GPL compliant licence"; (2) the licence page says nothing about bundled node groups, so that part of the claim rests on the asset metadata instead: the hair node groups shipped in 4.5.9 are stamped CC0 (measured), and their source repo blender-assets is CC0 1.0, so even copying the node groups themselves, not only their output, is unencumbered. Caveat on sources: the researcher's second URL (download.blender.org/release/GPL3-license.txt) returned 403 (Cloudflare challenge page) to both fetchers today, so it was not read; the GPLv3 text was read from Blender's source tree at doc/license/GPL3-license.txt instead. license.md on main (not 4.5.9) states "While Blender itself is released under GPU-GPL 3.0 or later" (sic), consistent with "v3 or later for distributions". The FAQ page footer notes it was edited 16 August 2024 to remove "remarks about game engine"; the licence pages contain no game-specific restriction. Blender in the container is the bpy 4.5 wheel, not a blender binary.

checks.notes: Every quoted phrase in the claim is verbatim on blender.org/about/license as of 2026-09-22, and the GPL-version split is exactly as stated (source: GPL v2 or later; "any distribution of Blender binaries": GPL v3 or later). Drift check: (1) the phrase "and its bundled node groups" is the researcher's extension; the licence page never mentions node groups, assets or bundled content. The extension nevertheless holds, on two independent grounds not cited by the researcher: the GNU FAQ says a GPL program's output is not covered by the program's licence, and the bundled hair node groups themselves are CC0 (LICENSE file shipped in Blender 4.5.9 datafiles/assets, and the 'CC0 - Public Domain' licence field on each hair node-group asset, read with bpy 4.5.9 in the comfyui-packaged container). So even the node groups could be redistributed, which is stronger than the claim needs. Recommend the register cite the CC0 LICENSE and the asset metadata for the node-group half of the claim rather than resting it on the "sole property" sentence alone. (2) The researcher's second URL, http://download.blender.org/release/GPL3-license.txt, returns HTTP 403 with a Cloudflare JavaScript challenge to non-browser clients (both WebFetch and curl), so I could not confirm its content; the same text is in Blender's own git tree at doc/license/GPL3-license.txt ("GNU GENERAL PUBLIC LICENSE Version 3, 29 June 2007"), readable via raw.githubusercontent.com. Suggest citing that path instead. (3) The Blender GitHub README says "Version 3" with no "or later"; not a contradiction, and it defers to blender.org/about/license for details. (4) The claim says "distributed" scripts; the page says "(if published)"; same meaning. (5) Minor wording: the page's exact phrase is "GNU GPL Version 2 or later" and "GNU GPL Version 3 or later"; the claim's parenthesis "(version 2 or later, v3 or later for distributions)" is a fair paraphrase. Not verified: the Blender manual's About > License page (Cloudflare-blocked), so I have no second copy of the "sole property" sentence, only the primary page plus the GNU FAQ as an independent source on output ownership. Web search budget was exhausted before this check, so no search was run; all URLs were direct fetches of known pages.

checks.evidence: license.txt, fetched raw 2026-09-22, line 1: "Copyright (c) 2020 Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. All rights reserved." Line 3 onward: "Permission is hereby granted, free of charge, to any person obtaining a copy of this software and associated documentation files (the "Software"), to deal in the Software without restriction, including without limitation the rights to use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense, and/or sell copies of the Software ... subject to the following conditions: The above copyright notice and this permission notice shall be included in all copies or substantial portions of the Software." This is the standard MIT text word for word. Repo metadata: "license": {"key": "mit", "name": "MIT License", "spdx_id": "MIT"}. TressFXAsset.cpp line 177: "bool TressFXAsset::GenerateFollowHairs(int numFollowHairsPerGuideHair, float tipSeparationFactor, float maxRadiusAroundGuideHair)". Lines 217-221: "Vector3 v01 = pos[indexRootVertMaster + 1] - pos[indexRootVertMaster]; v01.Normalize(); // Find two orthogonal unit tangent vectors to v01 ... GetTangentVectors(v01, t0, t1);". Line 231: "Vector3 offset = GetRandom(-maxRadiusAroundGuideHair, maxRadiusAroundGuideHair) * t0 + GetRandom(-maxRadiusAroundGuideHair, maxRadiusAroundGuideHair) * t1;". Lines 240-241: "float factor = tipSeparationFactor * ((float)k / ((float)m_numVerticesPerStrand)) + 1.0f; *followVert = *guideVert + offset * factor;".
checks.notes: Licence lens: the claim asserts only that TressFX is MIT-licensed and quotes the copyright line and the "free of charge" grant; both quotes are present verbatim (the copyright line continues "All rights reserved.", which the claim truncates but does not contradict). The claim makes no statement about what a shipped game may do beyond "MIT", so it does not exceed the text; the text itself grants use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense and sell subject to keeping the notice. The recursive tree (not truncated) holds exactly one licence file, license.txt. Two caveats for the researcher, neither refuting: (1) README.md line 117 is an AMD document disclaimer ("No license, including implied or arising by estoppel, to any intellectual property rights is granted by this document"); it disclaims the README as a grant, not the software licence. (2) .gitmodules pulls libs/cauldron from GPUOpen-LibrariesAndSDKs/Cauldron, whose licence was not checked here; anything built from the full checkout inherits it. Technical wording caveats, also not refuting: t0 and t1 are, per the code's own comment, "two orthogonal unit tangent vectors to v01", i.e. perpendicular to the root segment direction, which matches the claim's phrase; each random component is drawn independently in [-maxRadius, +maxRadius], so the offset lies in a square of half-width maxRadius on the t0/t1 plane rather than a disc, and its magnitude can reach maxRadius times root 2; the offset is also applied to every vertex of the follow strand scaled by 1 + tipSeparationFactor * k/n, so the root gets the raw offset and the tip a larger one. Randomness is rand()/RAND_MAX with no seeding in this file. Repo pushed_at 2023-01-26, not archived.

claims.claim: The Ward et al. hair-modelling survey (IEEE TVCG 2007, DOI 10.1109/TVCG.2007.30) states that uniform root distribution over the scalp 'makes a good approximation of real hair distribution', that 2D-map placement distorts on the curved scalp, which Bando et al. corrected with a harmonic mapping plus Poisson-disc spacing measured in world space, and that painted density maps give local thinning.

The Ward et al. survey describes three global-shape models: Anjyo's cantilever beam bending a pore-clamped strand under gravity; Hadap's fluid-flow styling, strands as streamlines around the head with user-placed 'streams, vortices and sources', a vortex making a curl; and Yu's static 3D vector fields, along which a strand grows from its scalp point by fixed steps to its length.

The Ward et al. survey's detail models: a wisp shaped by a master strand whose members vary by a length distribution, a deviation radius function and a fuzziness value (Choe); curls and waves as trigonometric offset functions with per-cluster random terms (Yu); and alpha-textured NURBS strips, 'limited due to the flat representation' until warped into a U-shape (Liang and Huang).

Bertails et al. (Super-Helices, SIGGRAPH 2006) parameterise curliness as kappa1 = 1/r_h, kappa2 = 0 and tau = Delta_h / (2 pi r_h^2), r_h and Delta_h being a real clump's helix radius and step measured near the tips, add small random variations per strand, and interpolate between guides fully near the scalp and not within a wisp near the tips.

Strands2Cards initialises each strip around its wisp's guide strand with normals propagated from the negative root Frenet normal by rotation-minimising frames, uses two strips per wisp rotated +45 and -45 degrees about the tangent for volumetric hair, starts at 0.1 cm strip width, and fits over 1000 steps against 13 orthographic 200 x 200 views of cluster-coloured coverage masks.

'Internal' is the page's own typo; the publications list says 'International'. The Wayback availability API returned no snapshot for a 2012 query, and my queries for other years returned empty bodies, so the earliest archived wording is not established. It declares GPL-2.0-or-later in blender_manifest.toml line 15, as an SPDX header on line 1 of every .py file checked, and as a README link to spdx.org; there is no LICENSE file and the GitHub API licence field is null (2026-09-22). __init__.py lines 3-4 also state that a portion is Antti Tikka's Modifier List code "used under the terms of the GNU General Public License v3", so the combined work is distributable only under GPL-3.0 terms. The README (line 40) says sales on Gumroad fund updates and the GitHub copy is "for educational use or testing purposes prior to purchase"; that is a stated intent, not a licence term (GPL-2.0 s6 forbids further restrictions), and the Gumroad page shows no licence text. Each card follows the cluster mean strand, framed by the Bishop formulas (Bergou et al. 2008, a parallel-transport frame the paper calls "a more numerically stable choice" than Frenet-Serret). The half-width at sample j is the largest binormal-direction distance from the mean sample to the member strands' sample j. The root normal is chosen by evenly sampling candidate normals on a circle (20 on a positive half-circle in v2) and keeping the one that minimises the projection loss. The quad strip is downsampled to n^q quads: 31 for standard cards, 15 for cross cards, 48 for Afro (v2 only; v1 leaves n^q unspecified). Cross cards pair two cards at a 90-degree angle to fake volume.

claims.claim: DiffHairCard uses a 2048 x 2048 atlas holding 32 card textures of 512 x 256, encodes strands as 2D splines in texture space, adds a hair cap and cross-cards for short or coily hair, fits 100 to 400 cards (100 in 46 minutes, 400 in about an hour, 7 to 10 GB memory), and no code release was found.

Houdini's Hair Card Generate SOP 'assigns groups of nearby curves to clusters and then generates polygon cards for each cluster', clustering by position at Curve Cluster Location (default 0.5) on groomed guides, with Number Hair Cards, Seed, Smooth Orientation, Width Method (explicit or from neighbouring cluster density) clamped by Width Max, Width Ramp taper, Divisions, Bend Range and Extra Length.

Houdini's Hair Card Texture tool renders the atlas with an orthographic camera into diffuse, alpha, ID, tip, depth and UV-bounds planes, and lays it out as four strip regions of a few hundred strips each, assigning every card to the region whose length-to-width proportion is closest so that stretching is minimised.

Hair Tool 4 (commercial, Blender 4.2 and above) distributes roots by Poisson sampling with a Min Distance, offers 2D UV patterns Hex, Fibonacci Disk, Fibonacci Square, Grid and Plastic, deforms strands with Set Radius, Align Tilt, Noise, Curls, Clump and Glue, and converts to cards through Flat, Circle, Braid and Curls profiles whose Tilt 'aligns tilt to hair source surface'.

claims.claim: The normal scalp whorl is a single clockwise whorl lateral to the midline in the parietal region just below the vertex, not at the top of the head; about 10 percent are counter-clockwise, 5 percent of people have two whorls, and 7.8 percent of 510 children had an additional frontal whorl.

A long hairstyle was built in five card layers (base covering the head, secondary layer diluting the shape, single silhouette cards on temples, bangs, braids and ponytail, micro-detail cards of 1 to 3 hairs, facial layer), so fringe and temples are their own card groups, which must share the flow field with the top at the parting.

Houdini's Guide Process Set Lift lifts curves off the skin or flattens them, randomised per curve, and Bend bends by an angle; Blender's Shrinkwrap Hair Curves holds curves at an Offset Distance from a surface with Lock Roots, and Hair Curves Noise displaces with a Shape falloff (0 constant, 0.5 linear root to tip) and Cumulative Offset.

Forum practice for keeping long hair out of the shoulders is a body collision proxy plus authoring: collision shapes over the body with a margin, hair raised by morphs or mesh edits if it starts inside the body, simulation started from a T-pose, and hair vertices weighted 100 percent to the head bone rather than neck or shoulder bones.

For stylised hair the structure is big, medium and small forms where the medium shapes are the clumps, made "a bit wider and flatter" so fewer strands cover a wider area, with thin strands on a rectangle bevel profile and strand count balanced between messy (too many) and clay-like (too few); no source read gave a card count or width.

A published hairline design method places the mid-frontal point 7.9 cm (8 cm plus or minus 1 cm in use) above the glabella in the midline, the frontotemporal point 7.9 cm from it (8 cm across and 8 cm above the lateral canthus), and the temporal peak 5 cm further towards the lateral canthus.

No open Blender tool found implements card layout: GBH Tool's hair-card feature is a texture-baking scene (orthographic camera, render passes), Daniel Bystedt's free hair-cards-from-curves setup (Blender 3.6+) deforms card meshes along curves with twist aligned to the surface but states no licence on the pages read, and Hair Tool is commercial.

Scalp density varies by region by tens of percent, not orders of magnitude (occipital 65 to 85 follicular units per cm2 at 1.0 to 1.4 mm spacing, temples sparsest), and a natural hairline ramps from about 20 to 30 grafts per cm2 at an undulating, intermittently thinned border to 40 to 50 in the frontal tuft.

HairGPT, following the Hairmony taxonomy, partitions the scalp into eight regions (Front, Top, Crown, Nape, Right Temple, Left Temple, Right Side, Left Side) and generates strands region by region in the order Front, Top, Crown, Nape, then sides and temples.

The single-image pipeline in arXiv 2608.13679 (Hao et al., "Strand-based Hairstyle Generation via Large Reconstruction and Multimodal Models") builds an orientation field on an LRM-reconstructed hair-surface mesh and its enclosed volume, not on the scalp. Image-space strand directions from LMM-generated grayscale guidance images are projected onto the hair surface as sign-free tensors (M = d d^T). An LMM marks parting lines (where hair separates into different flow directions) and constrained regions (ponytails, buns) on rendered views; these are projected onto the mesh, and graph edges that cross a parting spline are removed. Stage I smooths the tensor field over neighbouring surface vertices while pinning the tensors of vertices near the parting line to their projected values with weight w^p = 10^6. Stage II resolves sign per semantic region: in a gathering region (the surface between a parting line and its constrained structure) hair flows towards the interface with the constrained region; in the constrained region itself hair flows away from that interface; in a loose region hair flows away along gravity; signs are set on the boundary curves and propagated to neighbours, with the scalp excluded. Stage III diffuses the oriented field into the volume, softly constraining scalp vertices to the outward scalp normal (w^n = 10^6) and other surface vertices to their Stage II orientation (w^t = 10). Strands are then seeded on the scalp and advected until they reach the hair-volume boundary, followed by a gap-filling pass that traces bidirectionally from uncovered volume samples until one end reaches the scalp and the other the hair boundary.
claims.as_first_reported: A strand-generation pipeline builds the scalp flow field by marking parting lines where flow splits, smoothing the direction field between neighbours while pinning parting directions with weight 10^6, resolving sign by semantic rules (loose hair follows gravity, gathered hair flows towards its gathering), constraining scalp vertices to outward normals, and seeding roots then advecting strands until they leave the volume.

The paper (Hao, Huang, Shen, Wang, Zheng, Wu, LIGHTSPEED, "Strand-based Hairstyle Generation via Large Reconstruction and Multimodal Models", arXiv 2608.13679v1) does not build a "scalp flow field". Section 3.1: "we subtract the bust mesh from the full reconstruction to obtain a watertight hair mesh M^hair = M^full \ M^bust" and "We denote the enclosed hair volume by Omega." Section 3.2: image directions are projected onto "the hair mesh M^hair ... onto the tangent plane of the face". Section 3.4: "we sample the hair volume Omega using Poisson disk sampling. Let S^Omega = {s_i} denote the volumetric samples and V^surface = {v_i} the set of vertices on M^hair"; Stage I runs on "G^surface subset G ... the subgraph restricted to surface vertices" with the smoothing sum over (i,j) in G^surface. The scalp enters only as a mask "inherited from the aligned bust model" that provides "semantic guidance and boundary conditions" (3.1). Every other clause is supported verbatim: 3.3 "Parting line: a region on the scalp where hair separates into different flow directions"; Stage I pins the parting tensor with the term ||M_i - M_i^0||_F^2 over v_i in V_parting at w^p = 10^6; Stage II "In a gathering region, hair flows toward the interface shared with the associated constrained region. In a constrained region, hair flows away from that interface. In a loose region, hair flows away along the gravity direction."; Stage III "At the scalp, strand roots should emerge approximately along the outward scalp normal" with ||o_i - n_i||^2 over V^scalp at w^n = 10^6; 3.5 "We first seed strands on the scalp and advect them along the orientation field, following prior work." and "Tracing terminates when a strand reaches the boundary of the hair volume."
checks.notes: Conflation found: the claim collapses three surfaces into "the scalp". In the paper the parting lines are defined on the scalp, the smoothing and parting pins run on the LRM-reconstructed hair mesh surface, the diffusion runs on Poisson-disk samples inside the enclosed hair volume, and the scalp (a mask inherited from a fitted bust template) is only a boundary condition and seeding surface. For a re-implementation in this repo that matters: the method needs a reconstructed outer hair mesh and its interior, not just the 9.5 cm scalp sphere that make_hair.py grows from. Two omissions that do not contradict the claim: the third sign rule (constrained regions flow away from the interface) and the secondary gap-filling strands traced bidirectionally from unvisited volume samples "until one direction reaches the scalp, and the other reaches the hair boundary". The tracing step is credited to prior work by the authors themselves ("following prior work"), so it is not novel to this pipeline. Independence: single source. It is an arXiv preprint, v1 only, submitted 2026-08-13, cs.GR, no venue, no comments field, no project page, no code or weights link anywhere in the paper; Semantic Scholar records citationCount 0 (CorpusId 291167629). The claim is a fair reading of one unreviewed preprint, not an independently corroborated fact. Web search budget for this session was exhausted (200/200) before I could search for a second source, so the search for corroboration was limited to fetches of the arXiv HTML, the arXiv abs page, the arXiv API and the Semantic Scholar API; no second independent description of the method was found on those. The arXiv API "updated" date reads 2026-09-22 while the abs page lists only v1; I did not open a v2 because none is listed. Corrected wording: A strand-generation pipeline (arXiv 2608.13679v1) builds an orientation field over the reconstructed outer hair mesh and the hair volume it encloses, not over the scalp: it marks parting lines (regions on the scalp where flow splits), smooths a sign-invariant tensor field between neighbouring hair-mesh surface vertices while pinning the parting-region tensors to their projected values with weight 10^6, resolves sign by semantic rules (gathering regions flow towards the interface with their constrained region, constrained regions flow away from it, loose regions flow along gravity), diffuses the oriented field into the volume with scalp vertices pinned to outward scalp normals (weight 10^6), then seeds strands on the scalp and advects them along the field until they reach the boundary of the hair volume, with extra bidirectional strands filling unvisited volume samples.

claims.claim: Both tools clump by picking centre curves from the input at a minimum spacing (Blender Guide Distance, Houdini Clump Size), pulling each curve towards its centre with a strength (Blender Factor, Houdini Tightness plus Blend) shaped root to tip (Blender Shape, Houdini Clump Profile). Blender's Clump Hair Curves assigns every curve to its nearest guide (Create Guide Index Map) and adds random Tip Spread, but has no stray control and no iteration. Houdini's Hair Clump 2.0 (since 17.0) blends a curve between the clump curves that influence it, lets a Stray Rate percentage of curves escape by a Stray Amount, and its Fractal Clumping repeats for a set number of Iterations with Size Reduction and Tightness Reduction per iteration; it has no random tip spread parameter.
claims.as_first_reported: Production clumping (Blender's Clump Hair Curves, Houdini's Hair Clump) picks guide curves at a minimum Guide Distance or Clump Size, assigns each curve to a guide, pulls it in by a Factor with a root-to-tip Shape or Clump Profile, spreads tips randomly, lets a Stray percentage escape, and repeats with Size Reduction per iteration for sub-clumps.

No Stray input and no Iterations or Size Reduction input on either branch; the word "stray" and the word "iteration" do not occur on the page. Assignment to a guide is confirmed by Create Guide Index Map: "maps every hair curve to its nearest guide curve. Each non-guide curve is assigned the index of the guide curve it should follow." Houdini Hair Clump 2.0 (docs 22.0, 20.5 and 19.5, "Since 17.0", "Clumps guide curves together"): Clump Size ("When no clump curves are provided, uses a a set of curves from the first input with that are spaced such that clumps have roughly this size"), Blend, Tightness ("Controls how tightly curves are clumped"), Stray Amount, Stray Rate ("The percentage of curves to which are allowed to stray from their clump"), Stray Falloff, Clump Profile ("Controls the tightness of the clump along it's length"), Fractal Clumping: Iterations ("Clump this number of times"), Size Reduction ("Reduce clump size by this factor after each iteration"), Tightness Reduction, Goal Feedback. Houdini also blends a curve between several clump curves rather than assigning it to exactly one guide ("Method: Controls how clumps that influence a hair curve are blended", "Search Beyond Clump Radius", "Crossover Rate"), and its "guides" are the input curves, with the clump centres called "clump curves".

checks.notes: Refuted in part only, on names and one mechanism; the substance holds. (1) Blender has no parameter called "UV Mask Texture": the manual names it "Mask Texture" and says it is sampled using the Surface UV Map input. It also does not scale Density; it controls "which areas of the surface generate hair" and is sampled after root points are generated, i.e. it masks roots rather than scaling the scatter. (2) "N nearest guides" is supported: the parameter is "Interpolation Guides", described as the number of nearest guide curves. (3) Houdini's Relax Iterations text says it relaxes "guide locations after scattering"; since the node scatters "hair or guides", "relaxes roots" is a fair paraphrase but not the literal wording. (4) Houdini's guide blending is also governed by Influence Decay, Maximum Guide Count, Max Guide Angle and Blending Method, and Influence Radius itself is attribute- or texture-overridable; the claim's "blends guides by Influence Radius" is not wrong but is a subset. (5) The Houdini page is for Houdini 22.0, Hair Generate version 2.0 ("Since 17.0"); the Blender page is the main-branch manual source and states no version. claims.claim: Guide interpolation works from numpy guides: 40 hand-written guide curves with surface = scalp and surface_uv_map = 'UVMap', run through Attach Hair Curves to Surface (Snap to Surface, Sample Attachment UV) then Interpolate Hair Curves at Density 3000, evaluated headlessly to 419 curves x 6 points carrying guide_curve_index, surface_normal, rest_position and surface_uv_coordinate.

bpy.ops.curves in 4.5.9 has no curves-to-mesh operator (its list runs add_bezier through tilt_clear, including snap_curves_to_surface and surface_set), while bpy.ops.object.curves_empty_hair_add creates a CURVES object parented to the active mesh with Curves.surface, surface_uv_map copied from the active UV map and a plain 'Surface Deform' NODES modifier (measured: surface 'Scalp', surface_uv_map 'UVMap', parent 'Scalp').

The curves hair object, Add Empty Hair and geometry-nodes support arrived in Blender 3.3 (7 September 2022); the 26 hair node group assets and the Essentials library in 3.5 (29 March 2023); node group assets entered the Add Modifier menu in 4.0; 4.1 replaced Auto Smooth with the Smooth by Angle asset; 4.5 added Set Mesh Normal.

Card-atlas baking is exposed headlessly as bpy.ops.object.bake(type, pass_filter, use_selected_to_active, cage_extrusion, cage_object, normal_space, target, margin, ...) with types including Combined, Ambient Occlusion, Normal, UV, Emit, Diffuse and Glossy; the manual says Selected to Active rays 'are cast from the low-poly object inwards' and baking 'requires a mesh to have a UV map', but no bake was run here.

Cycles renders curves objects as 'Rounded Ribbons' ('flat ribbon with rounded normals, for fast rendering') or '3D Curves' ('circular 3D geometry'), and the container's Cycles add-on is registered with get_devices() listing ('NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4070 Ti SUPER', 'CUDA') and ('Intel Core i7-14700K', 'CPU'); this is the strand look a bake would capture, unrelated to how the card is shaded.

checks.notes: Drift/conflation findings: (1) No product or version conflation found; the pipeline is 4.5-specific and the container is 4.5.9, but the claim does not say the minimum version. (2) Radius handling changed at 4.5: before, Curve to Mesh scaled the profile by the radius attribute implicitly; in 4.5 the Scale field defaults to 1.0 and ignores radius, so "Scale = Radius" is a required explicit link, correct as written. (3) "to_mesh(), bpy.ops.wm.obj_export" reads as a chain, but to_mesh's own doc says the result "is temporary and cannot be used by objects from the main database"; the exporter evaluates scene objects itself (apply_modifiers default True, export_eval_mode default DAG_EVAL_VIEWPORT). In the researcher's runs to_mesh() was the measurement step, so this is loose wording, not an error. Exporting the whole scene silently skips the Curves object (only 'o Host' written). (4) Naming: the asset is 'Interpolate Hair Curves' ("Interpolates existing guide curves on a surface mesh"), catalogued Hair-Generation; Clump/Curl/Braid are Hair-Guides; the deformers are the Hair-Deformation catalog. "Interpolate from guides" is a paraphrase, not the asset name. (5) "every step verified headless except export": the researcher's MESH-host graph runs (17:00 and 17:03) did not contain the Store Named Attribute 'UVMap' node; that node was run at 16:53 in a sibling graph (bpy.ops.object.convert of a CURVES object, after to_mesh failed on it with "Object does not have geometry data", which is why the recommendation moved to a MESH host). claims.claim: Generate, Interpolate and Attach Hair Curves to Surface 'will not function without the Surface geometry/object and Surface UV Map inputs'; each has two 'Surface' sockets (Geometry, then Object) that must be chosen by socket_type, and on a modifier the UV map is passed as m[ident + '_use_attribute'] = True plus m[ident + '_attribute_name'] = 'UVMap', an int raising TypeError.

Generate Hair Curves exposes inputs Surface (Geometry), Surface (Object), Surface UV Map, Surface Rest Position, Hair Length, Hair Material, Control Points, Poisson Disk Distribution, Density, Density Mask, Mask Texture, Viewport Amount and Seed, emits straight segments along the surface normal, and its output carries id, rest_position, surface_normal, UVMap and surface_uv_coordinate attributes.

Set Hair Curve Profile (Replace Radius, Radius, Shape, Factor Min, Factor Max) writes the point-domain 'radius' attribute, giving 0.0 to 0.007 for Radius 0.007 and Shape 0.5, and Clump Hair Curves (Guide Distance 0.02, Factor 0.8) plus Hair Curves Noise on 421 curves evaluated in 0.01 s while adding a 'guide_curve_index' attribute.

Blender 4.5 documents that Curve to Mesh extrudes the profile curve along every spline and that its Scale input is "the scale used at each control point of the input curve to scale the profile curve", replacing the implicit use of the "radius" attribute (4.5 release notes); Set Curve Normal in Free mode takes a Normal input that becomes the custom_normal used as the final curve normal, and must be set after any rotation. Which profile axis faces the curve normal is not in the manual: the 4.5 source (build_point_matrix in blenkernel/intern/curve_to_mesh_convert.cc) maps profile X to the curve normal, profile Y to normalize(cross(tangent, normal)) and profile Z to the tangent, and scales the profile uniformly by Scale (default 1.0, no radius fallback). It follows, not from the cited pages but from that code, that a Curve Line profile from (0,-1,0) to (0,1,0) with the outward direction fed to Set Curve Normal (Free) and Scale linked to Radius yields a ribbon of width 2 x Scale lying in the plane of the tangent and binormal, i.e. facing the fed normal, and a 2 m wide ribbon when Scale is left at its default. The figures |dot(face normal, radial)| mean 1.0 for the Y profile, 0.0 for the X profile, and widths 0.014 m root, 0.005 m tip and 2.0 m without Scale are the researcher's own container measurement on 300 numpy strands (no source, script or output available), not a documented value.

checks.notes: Refuted in part, on the fact-against-source lens: the three cited sources say something narrower than the claim. They support that the profile is extruded and scaled per control point, that Scale replaces the implicit radius in 4.5, and that Free mode uses the Normal input; they do not state the profile-axis-to-normal mapping that makes a Y-line profile lie flat, nor width = 2 x radius, nor any of the numbers. The mechanism is nonetheless correct against a primary source the researcher did not cite (the 4.5 blenkernel and node source, opened above), and the "2.0 m without Scale" figure follows from Scale's default of 1.0 and a 2-unit profile, again from source code rather than the manual. Two caveats the claim omits: the source comment says "Normal and tangent may not be orthogonal in case of custom normals", and z_axis = normal is used unorthogonalised, so a fed direction not perpendicular to the strand tangent shears the card and |dot| falls below 1 (the measured mean 1.0 is presumably rounded); and the manual requires custom normals to be set after any rotation. The measured values cannot be verified here because the run is not in the repo; re-measuring in the Blender container was outside this lens and was not done. The rendered manual pages returned HTTP 403 to WebFetch and curl but opened in the Playwright browser; their text matches the 4.5-release RST in the blender-manual repository word for word. Corrected wording: Blender 4.5 documents that Curve to Mesh extrudes the profile curve along every spline and that its Scale input is "the scale used at each control point of the input curve to scale the profile curve", replacing the implicit use of the "radius" attribute (4.5 release notes); Set Curve Normal in Free mode takes a Normal input that becomes the custom_normal used as the final curve normal, and must be set after any rotation. Which profile axis faces the curve normal is not in the manual: the 4.5 source (build_point_matrix in blenkernel/intern/curve_to_mesh_convert.cc) maps profile X to the curve normal, profile Y to normalize(cross(tangent, normal)) and profile Z to the tangent, and scales the profile uniformly by Scale (default 1.0, no radius fallback). It follows, not from the cited pages but from that code, that a Curve Line profile from (0,-1,0) to (0,1,0) with the outward direction fed to Set Curve Normal (Free) and Scale linked to Radius yields a ribbon of width 2 x Scale lying in the plane of the tangent and binormal, i.e. facing the fed normal, and a 2 m wide ribbon when Scale is left at its default. The figures |dot(face normal, radial)| mean 1.0 for the Y profile, 0.0 for the X profile, and widths 0.014 m root, 0.005 m tip and 2.0 m without Scale are the researcher's own container measurement on 300 numpy strands (no source, script or output available), not a documented value.

claims.claim: The Blender 4.5 API docs cited say only that Object.to_mesh() creates "a Mesh data-block from the current state of the object", that bpy.data.meshes.new_from_object() adds "a new mesh created from given object (... final evaluated geometry, with all modifiers etc., if object is evaluated)", and that bpy.ops.object.convert(target='MESH') makes "Mesh from Curve, Surface, Metaball, Text, or Point Cloud objects" (a Curves hair object is not among the listed sources). None of the three pages contains the string "Object does not have geometry data", mentions Curves objects, Curve to Mesh, Object Info, an empty evaluated Curves block, vertex or face counts, or UV retention. LICENSE.md C: "Clothes (any MHCLO-based asset) ... released under CC0 1.0 Universal"; D: "Exports to files (FBX, OBJ, DAE, MHX2...) ... We regard these things as your data". (2) The zip's own mhclo headers contradict CC0 for 12 of 25: 10 say "# license AGPL3 (see also http://www.makehuman.org/doc/node/external_tools_license.html)" (culturalibre_hair_01/02, elvs_double_mh_braid, elvs_french_braid_variation, elvs_unkempt_french_braid, learning_anime_hair, littleright_bobcut_hair, rehmanpolanski_hair_bun_brown, sonntag78 x2), elvs_reverse_french_braid_bun says "# license CC_by", o4saken_long01 says "# author 04saken / # license CC BY 4.0"; 13 say CC0 or CC-0. (3) o4saken_long01 (node/1471): "Submitted by punkduck", description "The real author of this asset is o4saken ... I only changed a few vertices", listed "License: CC0"; the same uploader's sibling o4saken_curly01 with the same origin ("The texture is identically to the O4saken curly01 version") is listed "License: CC-BY - Creative Commons Attribution"; no original o4saken upload found on the repository (clothes listing pages 0 to 22). The hair01 half overstates in three ways: "every mhmat header" is false (5 of 25), the "no attribution" and "copied through some other means" sentences are scoped to "core assets" and the project itself says repository assets may differ, and the zip's mhclo headers carry AGPL3/CC-BY lines the researcher did not mention. The AGPL3 lines are most likely stale MakeClothes boilerplate (the repository pages set by the same authors say CC0), but the page they cite is gone, so this cannot be shown from text. The one asset with a genuine provenance problem is o4saken_long01. For the repo's purposes: ship the 10 system hairs freely; for hair01, rely on the repository entry per asset and either drop o4saken_long01 or credit o4saken under CC-BY. Corrected wording: MakeHuman's makehuman_system_assets pack (10 hair assets: afro01, bob01, bob02, braid01, long01, ponytail01, short01 to short04) is CC0: every one of its mhmat and mhclo headers says the asset "was explicitly released as CC0 in september 2020" naming the copyright holders, the pack page lists CC0 for every row, the licence page says core assets need no payment, copyright notice or attribution, LICENSE.md says exports are "your data", and the FAQ says core assets impose no restriction whether "used through MakeHuman or copied through some other means". The hair01 community pack (25 hair assets by 10 authors) is LABELLED CC0 by the pack page's licence column, by packs/hair01.json and by the asset repository entries checked (chosen by the uploading author), but those "core asset" statements do not cover it (LICENSE.md and the MPFB FAQ say third-party repository assets may carry a different licence and are the user's responsibility); only 5 of its 25 mhmat headers say CC0 (20 say nothing), its mhclo headers say AGPL3 for 10 assets and CC-BY for 2, and o4saken_long01 was uploaded as CC0 by punkduck, who states the real author is o4saken, whose sibling upload is CC-BY and whose mhclo says "author 04saken, license CC BY 4.0", so that asset should be treated as CC-BY at best and the 24 others as CC0 on the strength of the repository entries, with the header contradictions recorded.

checks.notes: Drift and conflation found: (1) the claim runs the system pack (headers, json, page and LICENSE.md all agree) together with the community pack (json and repository pages say CC0; file headers disagree in 12 mhclo and are silent in 20 mhmat). (2) "the FAQ says copying assets out of MakeHuman is unrestricted" is a paraphrase of a sentence about "core assets"; the same site and LICENSE.md section D explicitly carve out third-party repository assets, which is exactly what hair01 is. (3) The researcher's three cited URLs contain no FAQ text; the FAQ sentence is at https://static.makehumancommunity.org/makehuman/faq/are_makehuman_files_free.html (page dated Oct 17, 2017), which they did not list. (4) The zip's Last-Modified is 2024-04-14; it has not changed since the researcher's unpack. (5) The makehuman-assets GitHub repo the system headers refer to ("license text ... in the root of this repository") returns 404 on the GitHub API today; the CC0 text is instead in makehumancommunity/makehuman LICENSE.ASSETS.md. (6) Second independent source for the system pack CC0: MPFB's locally installed copy of the same 10 assets carries identical headers, and the GitHub commit history dates the relicensing to 2020-09-26. Web search budget was exhausted this session, so every check above was by direct fetch, file download or local file read. Practical consequence for the repo: the system hair is clean to ship; for hair01, if any asset is used, record the repository page URL as the licence source and note the stale in-file header, or strip the header on import. Corrected wording: MakeHuman's makehuman_system_assets pack (10 hair assets: afro01, bob01, bob02, braid01, long01, ponytail01, short01 to short04) is CC0: every one of its mhmat and mhclo headers says it was "explicitly released as CC0 in september 2020", the pack page lists all 94 assets as CC0, the project's LICENSE.md (commit 2020-09-26) puts all MHCLO-based bundled assets under CC0 1.0 Universal, the licence page says no attribution or copyright notice is needed, and the FAQ "Are MakeHuman files free?" says copying the core assets out "through some other means" imposes no restriction. The hair01 community pack (25 hair assets by 10 third-party authors) is listed as CC0 on its pack page, in packs/hair01.json inside hair01_cc0.zip, and on each asset's repository page; but the files themselves are not consistent: 20 of 25 mhmat files carry no licence line, and 12 of 25 mhclo headers still carry older MakeClothes-era strings (10 "license AGPL3", one "CC_by", one "CC BY 4.0") that contradict the repository listing and point at dead makehuman.org URLs. The CC0 status of hair01 rests on the uploader's declaration on the repository page and the curated pack json, not on the file headers, and the "core assets" FAQ wording does not cover third-party assets.

checks.notes: Core claim holds exactly and does not overstate what a game may do: CC0 1.0 section 2 waives rights "for any purpose whatsoever, including without limitation commercial, advertising or promotional purposes"; section 4(a) keeps trademark and patent rights, which is irrelevant to shipping node-generated geometry. Stronger source than the researcher gave: Blender's own repo at v4.5.0 carries assets/LICENSE (CC0 1.0 Universal) directly beside the published assets/geometry_nodes/procedural_hair_node_assets.blend (132 bytes in the API listing, so an LFS pointer). Precision corrections to the researcher's evidence, none of which change the verdict: (1) "CC0 1.0 Universal" is line 3 of LICENSE, line 1 is "Creative Commons Legal Code"; (2) the Snow credit line on the page reads "Snow Rig (CC) Blender Foundation | studio.blender.org", with "(CC)" not "©"; (3) Ellie's page requires attribution to Blender Studio but gives no fixed credit-line string, unlike Snow and Rain, so "with a required credit line" is exact for Snow and Rain and only "attribution required" for Ellie; (4) README line 11 says "Copyright: keep the field empty", yet the shipped file has copyright 'Blender Foundation', so the claim describes the file, not the README's instruction; (5) the file lives at work/bundled/nodes/ in blender-assets, not under publish/ (publish/ holds only online assets). The studio terms page adds a general default: "Unless notified otherwise, all digital content (webpages, video, artwork, 3D data) is available under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0." Blender's about/license page does not mention bundled assets at all (not found). Also note the node groups produce curve geometry; the CC0 status covers the node-group assets themselves, and any hair geometry generated by them is the user's own output per blender.org/about/license ("What you create with Blender is your sole property").

Neither Mixamo nor Ready Player Me is a hair source: Mixamo's Adobe-hosted FAQ allows free commercial use but prohibits 'Any type of free distribution of character or animation raw files', and Ready Player Me wound down its services on 31 January 2026, with readyplayer.me and docs.readyplayer.me resolving to no DNS address on 2026-09-22.

Neither Kenney's CC0 character packs nor KayKit's CC0 Adventurers pack contains 3D hair: Kenney's character-female-a.glb holds only 'body-mesh' (578 triangles) and 'head-mesh' (298 triangles) with an opaque 'colormap' material, and KayKit's Knight.glb nodes are head, helmet, cape, body, limbs and rig bones with one 'knight_texture' material, no file named 'hair'.

OpenGameArt's CC0 3D hair meshes are few and old: Micket's 2013 .blend hairstyles are low-poly shells of 253 (long male, hair.png without working alpha), 201 (side parting), 236 (upcomb) and 867 (female ponytail) triangles, and Chloe Wolfe's 'Ponytail Hair - Chibi 3DM Collection' is CC-BY 3.0 / CC-BY-SA 3.0 / GPL / OGA-BY, not CC0.

Four Blender hair-generator add-ons on GitHub are generators, not drop-in assets, with GPL or no licence: GixoXYZ/BlenderGBHTool (57 stars, pushed 2024-11-21) is GPL-2.0-or-later and lists 'hair cards for video games', Mateusz-Dera/Anime-Hair-Generator is GPL-3.0, s-nako/HairArranger (curve-bevel anime hair) declares no licence, and Greg-Aster/Blender-Generate-Hair-as-Mesh-add-on shows an MIT badge but has no licence file.

Copyright is waived, and there is no particular limit when using them." followed by the list "Base models / Sample models / ・HairSample_Male / ・HairSample_Female / ・β Ver AvatarSample_1 [...] _4". OpenGameArt page: "License(s): CC0", "Author: VRoid Project (Submitted by hecko)", description "These models come from the alpha versions of VRoid Studio and were explicitly released by VRoid under CC0. They were downloaded from here where possible: https://vroid.pixiv.help/hc/en-us/articles/4402614652569-...", file "hairsample_female.zip 14.3 Mb". Parsed VRM 0.x meta from HairSample_Female.vrm: title "HairSample_Female", author "VRoidプロジェクト", licenseName "CC0", allowedUserName "Everyone", commercialUssageName "Allow", violentUssageName "Allow", sexualUssageName "Allow", otherPermissionUrl and otherLicenseUrl both "https://hub.vroid.com/license?allowed_to_use_user=everyone&characterization_allowed_user=everyone&corporate_commercial_use=allow&credit=unnecessary&modification=allow&personal_commercial_use=profit&redistribution=allow&sexual_expression=allow&version=1&violent_expression=allow"; exporterVersion "VRoidStudio-0.14.0".
checks.notes: All four parts of the claim are in the primary text or file, and the claim makes no statement about what a shipped game may do beyond what the pages say, so it is confirmed. Three precision points for whoever writes this up. (1) The guidelines qualify the ownership clause with "created from scratch"; the claim's "hair meshes you create" drops that qualifier, and a hair mesh made by editing a pixiv preset is pixiv content under the next sentence. Safer wording: "hair meshes you create from scratch belong to you". (2) The application ban has a self-use exemption ("only intended for use by you yourself") that the claim omits; omission narrows rather than overstates, so no refutation. (3) "Redistribution and modification allowed" is not a VRM 0.x meta field; it is carried by the query parameters modification=allow and redistribution=allow in otherPermissionUrl/otherLicenseUrl, which is still metadata inside the file. Correction to the researcher's evidence note: the FAQ does NOT list only AvatarSample_1 to _4 as CC0; it explicitly lists HairSample_Male and HairSample_Female (and "Base models") under "CC0 license models", so the mapping from the OpenGameArt file to pixiv's CC0 statement is confirmed by pixiv's own page, not unconfirmed. Context that resolves the apparent tension in the claim: the FAQ sits in the "VRoid Studio old beta > Sample Models for old beta" section and the file was exported by VRoidStudio-0.14.0, while the guidelines (edited 2023-12-21) describe content in the current Studio ("the base models when creating a new avatar"). Both statements are pixiv's; they refer to different content. Note the same FAQ lists old-beta "Base models" as CC0 while the guidelines say current base models are not, so base_female/base_male on OpenGameArt should not be read as covering current Studio base meshes. Not checked: the VRoid Studio Terms of Use Article 11 itself, the per-model FAQ articles for AvatarSample_1 to _4 (the FAQ gives no separate article for HairSample_Female), and whether the OpenGameArt zip is byte-identical to a file pixiv hosted.

checks.notes: Every named element of the claim (operator labels and ids, 10-point resample, 3x3 Mesh Grid, tangent-driven rotation, Scale Elements 0.2, density-driven Delete Geometry, Realize Instances, alpha=True image saved as PNG, Alpha linked to Principled Alpha, commented-out panel with a "TODO: Port cards" comment) is verbatim in the sources. Nuances that do not contradict the wording: (1) the generate operator first tries to load a pre-authored "{hair_asset}_cards" object from data/hair/haireditor/{hair_asset}.blend and only builds the geometry-nodes cards if that load fails, so the procedural path is the fallback; (2) the actual node chain order is Instance on Points -> Scale Elements -> Realize Instances -> Delete Geometry, whereas the claim lists Delete before Realize (the claim does not assert an order); (3) the full comment is "# TODO: Port cards, delete etc" (the claim truncates it); (4) the bake renders the hair curves through a Ray Portal BSDF card material with a Holdout on the Human, hidden other objects, two temporary 1000 W point lights, Cycles samples from a scene property (default 32) at a resolution property (default 1024), then saves to {hair_asset}_texture.png; (5) the panel button text would be "Convert to cards" and "Bake cards", while the operators' bl_labels are "Generate hair cards" and "Bake hair cards"; (6) the 2.0.11 release notes credit Klecer's thesis but do not mention cards or baking at all; (7) the haireditor asset-pack page names no licence, and GitHub's licence detection for the repo reports spdx NOASSERTION (repo LICENSE file not opened in this check), so the code's licence should be read from the file before anything is adapted rather than merely run. Nothing was executed; all evidence is read, not run.

checks.notes: Every element of the claim is supported by the source at the level of code, and by one genuinely independent source (the thesis PDF on BUT DSpace), so this is not a single-source claim. Tightenings, none of which changes the verdict: (1) The exact comment is "# TODO: Port cards, delete etc" (the claim's quote is a truncation). (2) The bake operator's idname is mpfb.bake_hair_operator, not a *_cards_* name; the claim only gives its label, which is exact. (3) If the node list in the claim is read as an order, Realize Instances comes before Delete Geometry in the code, not after. (4) "Rotated by tangent" summarises a Vector Rotate of the curve tangent about itself (a no-op rotation) fed as the Instance on Points Rotation input; that is what the code does. (5) "Bakes strands to an RGBA PNG": the code creates an alpha-enabled image, saves as PNG and wires Alpha into Principled Alpha. Whether the saved PNG's alpha actually carries a strand mask after a Cycles GLOSSY/DIFFUSE bake was not run by me (read, not run); the thesis itself cites a community "Bake Textures With Alpha Transparency" fix as reference [5], and the commented panel warns "baking process is slow and might crash blender". (6) Not in the claim but material to the repo's use: the generate operator first tries to load a pre-made "{hair_asset}_cards" object from data/hair/haireditor/{hair_asset}.blend and only builds the Geometry Nodes cards if none is found; both operators require the active object to be named 'Human' with the hair as its child, and they are reachable only via bpy.ops or F3 since no panel draws them. Drift checks: files exist on master and on the tagged releases v2.0.14 and v2.0.17 (2.0.11 has no git tag, so it was not checked at that exact release); PRs #262 and #276 landed on branch TomasKlecer_stage_hair_merge, which has diverged from master (ahead 16, behind 274), and even there the card UI stays commented. Licence: LICENSE.md says GPLv3 for the source; the haireditor asset pack page states no licence for hair.blend/fur.blend in its body (I did not download haireditor.zip, so the researcher's "no licence file" is neither confirmed nor refuted here). Release notes 2.0.11 credit the thesis but describe only curve hair, so the cards capability rests on the code and the thesis, not on any release note or docs page. No forum or blog post was involved.

On 2026-09-23 the owner called off the procedural hair generator as the route for hair and beards, after looking at the settled generator on the figure beside a Virt-A-Mate groom on the same figure at the same framing. The owner's words: the procedural results "still look terrible", and the route is now "hair objs instead. same with beards". This is the owner's decision and not a measurement. The generator is not deleted and scripts/make_hair.py still runs.

Probed per node on 2026-09-23 in Blender 4.5.9 in the comfyui-packaged container: Shrinkwrap Hair Curves is a projection, not a collision. It wrapped a straight 17 cm strand down to a median of 2.72 cm on the first pass, and a Restore Curve Segment Length after it re-extended a crumpled strand, so the turning angle climbed 4 to 12 to 38 degrees over successive passes and the reach over length fell to 0.44. A strand groom built on the bundled CC0 hair node groups was rejected on that measurement.

claims.claim: The comb is the styled pose, not the gravity: a solver refines an authored pose and does not replace the authoring, the way a Virt-A-Mate creator combs the guides and the solver only refines them. Measured on the bob on 2026-09-23 by running all three combinations: comb only, the behaviour before that session, spans 27.58 x 23.18 x 25.03 cm; comb then settle spans 26.42 x 23.78 x 24.07 cm at 13.8 degrees of turn; settle alone with the comb removed spans 31.00 x 23.92 x 28.15 cm at 23.9 degrees, which failed the generator's own acceptance test because the bounding box grew. Dropping main rigidity to 0.10 brought the span under the baseline but took the turning angle to 10.1 degrees, which is the wave ironed flat.
sources: scripts/make_hair.py, run on the host python3 with numpy 2.3.5 on 2026-09-23

claims.claim: A solver cannot fix a representation problem. At the same camera and framing on 2026-09-23 the settled procedural hair is 310 cards and the settled procedural beard 160 cards, against a Virt-A-Mate hair of 4,005 curves from 267 guides and a Virt-A-Mate beard of 12,969 curves from 1,179 guides, so every silhouette edge is a card edge and a card is centimetres wide on an 18 cm head.
Judge hair by looking at it on the figure, not by its numbers: every acceptance test passed on the run the owner rejected on 2026-09-23.
